Suspect infective endocarditis in anyone with fever and a predisposing condition (prosthetic valve, prior IE, injection drug use, structural heart disease, intracardiac device, long-term venous catheter or hemodialysis), a new regurgitant murmur, an unexplained embolic event, or bacteremia with a typical organism.

Diagnosis

  1. Blood cultures first: at least 3 sets from separate venipunctures before antibiotics. In a stable patient, waiting the short time needed to draw them is worth it; in septic shock, draw them quickly and start antibiotics without delay.
  2. Echocardiography: transthoracic echo (TTE) is the first imaging test. Go on to transesophageal echo (TEE) when TTE is negative but suspicion stays high, when the patient has a prosthetic valve or device, when S. aureus bacteremia is present, or when a complication (abscess, perforation) is suspected. TEE is more sensitive for small vegetations and for perivalvular abscess.
  3. Diagnostic criteria (modified Duke, updated as Duke-ISCVID 2023): major criteria are microbiological (typical organisms in separate cultures, or positive Coxiella serology) and imaging evidence (vegetation, abscess, new dehiscence of a prosthetic valve; cardiac CT or PET-CT can count). Minor criteria are a predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunologic phenomena and microbiology that falls short of major.
A positive culture for S. aureus, viridans streptococci, S. gallolyticus, HACEK organisms or community-acquired enterococci in a febrile patient is IE until proven otherwise. S. aureus bacteremia always gets an echocardiogram.

Empiric and directed antibiotics

SituationUsual approach
Native valve, empiric (stable)IV vancomycin (covers MRSA and streptococci), often with ceftriaxone; narrow when cultures return
Prosthetic valve, empiricVancomycin plus gentamicin, with rifampin added once staphylococcal infection is confirmed
MSSAAn antistaphylococcal β-lactam (nafcillin, oxacillin or cefazolin); it outperforms vancomycin
MRSAVancomycin or daptomycin
Penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci, S. gallolyticusPenicillin G or ceftriaxone
E. faecalisAmpicillin plus ceftriaxone (avoids aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity) or ampicillin plus gentamicin

Therapy usually lasts 4–6 weeks; prosthetic valve infection needs at least 6 weeks. Repeat blood cultures until they are negative; the duration counts from the first negative set. Selected stable patients with left-sided IE who have responded to IV therapy can complete the course with oral antibiotics, an option now supported by trial evidence.

Indications for surgery

  • Heart failure caused by valve dysfunction (for example acute severe aortic or mitral regurgitation): the most common and most urgent indication.
  • Uncontrolled infection: perivalvular abscess, fistula, new heart block, enlarging vegetation, or bacteremia persisting beyond about 5–7 days of appropriate therapy.
  • Organisms hard to cure medically: fungi, multidrug-resistant organisms, most prosthetic valve S. aureus infections.
  • Embolic risk: a large mobile vegetation (over about 10 mm) with an embolic event despite therapy.
New PR prolongation in a patient with aortic valve endocarditis is not a curiosity: it suggests a root abscess reaching the conduction system. Get a TEE and a surgical opinion.

After the diagnosis

  • S. gallolyticus → colonoscopy. Enterococcus → look for a GU or GI source.
  • Right-sided IE in people who inject drugs: treat the addiction too (offer medication for opioid use disorder) and plan harm reduction.
  • Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs do not prevent emboli in IE and raise the risk of bleeding into embolic strokes.

Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures

Prophylaxis is limited to patients at the highest risk of a bad outcome, before dental work that manipulates the gingiva or the periapical region or perforates the oral mucosa:

  • prosthetic valve, transcatheter valve, or prosthetic material used for valve repair;
  • previous infective endocarditis;
  • unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, a repair with prosthetic material in the first 6 months, or a residual defect next to prosthetic material;
  • cardiac transplant with valve disease.

The usual regimen is a single oral dose of amoxicillin 30–60 minutes before the procedure; alternatives for penicillin allergy include cephalexin (if the reaction was not anaphylaxis), azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline. Clindamycin is no longer advised. Mitral prolapse, a bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic disease without a prosthesis, and GI or GU procedures do not call for prophylaxis.

s23b-s-080101-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Acute myocarditis

Think of myocarditis in a young patient with chest pain or new heart failure after a viral illness, a raised troponin and nonobstructed coronary arteries.

  • Tests: ECG (sinus tachycardia, ST changes, arrhythmia), troponin, echocardiogram (global or regional dysfunction). Cardiac MRI is the best noninvasive test (myocardial edema and late gadolinium enhancement in a non-coronary pattern). Coronary angiography or CT angiography excludes infarction when the picture is uncertain. Endomyocardial biopsy is kept for fulminant disease, unexplained heart failure with ventricular arrhythmia or high-grade block, or suspected giant cell myocarditis.
  • Management: supportive, with guideline-directed therapy for reduced ejection fraction; mechanical support for fulminant shock. Avoid competitive sport for about 3–6 months and until testing has normalised. Immunosuppression is reserved for specific types (giant cell, eosinophilic, sarcoid, immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis).

Lyme carditis

  • Suspect it in a patient from a Ixodes area with palpitations, syncope or dyspnea weeks after erythema migrans; the ECG shows AV block that may fluctuate.
  • Admit and monitor patients who are symptomatic or who have a PR interval of 300 ms or more, second- or third-degree block. Give IV ceftriaxone and switch to oral doxycycline (or amoxicillin) when the block improves, for about 14–21 days in total. Mild first-degree block can be treated with oral antibiotics as an outpatient.
  • Use a temporary pacemaker for unstable high-grade block; a permanent pacemaker is almost never needed because the block resolves.

Chagas cardiomyopathy

  • Screen people who grew up in endemic rural Latin America who present with cardiomyopathy, RBBB with left anterior fascicular block, ventricular arrhythmia or stroke from an apical aneurysm. Diagnosis in the chronic phase is serologic (two different IgG assays); blood smears help only in the acute phase.
  • Treat heart failure as for other cardiomyopathies; anticoagulate for apical thrombus or embolism; ICD for sustained ventricular arrhythmia. Antiparasitic therapy (benznidazole, nifurtimox) is recommended for acute, congenital and reactivated disease and for children and women of reproductive age with chronic infection (it reduces congenital transmission); it is avoided in pregnancy.
  • Screen the patient's siblings and children, and the infants of infected mothers.

Syphilitic aortitis

  • Presents as ascending aortic aneurysm or aortic regurgitation in an older adult; linear calcification of the ascending aorta on imaging.
  • Confirm syphilis with treponemal and nontreponemal tests, and examine the CSF if there are neurologic signs. Treat tertiary (non-neurologic) syphilis with benzathine penicillin G IM weekly for 3 weeks; neurosyphilis needs IV aqueous penicillin G. Large aneurysms and severe regurgitation are repaired surgically.
A young adult with chest pain, ST elevation and a normal coronary angiogram after a "flu" probably has myocarditis, not an infarction. Do not give fibrinolytics without imaging evidence of coronary occlusion, and remember cocaine and coronary spasm as alternatives.

s23b-s-080102-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Recognise it

Suspect acute rheumatic fever in a child or young adult with fever and migratory large-joint arthritis, a new murmur, chorea or the characteristic skin signs 2–4 weeks after a sore throat. The diagnosis needs evidence of a recent group A streptococcal infection plus the right combination of major and minor manifestations (revised Jones criteria; the thresholds are lower in high-incidence populations).

Workup

  • Antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers (the most sensitive evidence when cultures are negative); throat culture or rapid antigen test.
  • ESR and CRP; ECG (PR prolongation is a minor criterion and can fluctuate).
  • Echocardiography with Doppler in every suspected case: it detects subclinical valvulitis (pathologic mitral or aortic regurgitation) and counts as carditis.

Treat the acute illness

  • Eradicate the streptococcus even if the throat culture is negative: a dose of IM benzathine penicillin G (or 10 days of oral penicillin or amoxicillin).
  • Arthritis and fever: aspirin or an NSAID such as naproxen; a dramatic response supports the diagnosis.
  • Carditis with heart failure: diuretics, ACE inhibitors and bed rest; glucocorticoids are sometimes used for severe carditis but have not been shown to prevent later valve disease. Surgery is needed for rare ruptured chordae or severe acute regurgitation.
  • Chorea: usually self-limited; valproate or carbamazepine for disabling movements.

Prevent the first attack and recurrences

  • Primary prevention: treat streptococcal pharyngitis (confirmed by rapid test or culture) with penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days, or one IM benzathine penicillin dose. Treatment started within about 9 days of symptom onset prevents ARF. Penicillin allergy: cephalexin (non-anaphylactic allergy), azithromycin or clindamycin.
  • Secondary prevention after a diagnosis of ARF: IM benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks (every 3 weeks in high-risk settings). Typical durations:
HistoryContinue prophylaxis
ARF without carditis5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer
Carditis without residual valve disease10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer
Carditis with residual valve disease10 years or until age 40, whichever is longer; sometimes for life

Rheumatic mitral stenosis in adults

  • Typical patient: a woman from a high-prevalence region with exertional dyspnea, atrial fibrillation or hemoptysis; a loud S1, opening snap and low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex.
  • Atrial fibrillation with rheumatic mitral stenosis needs a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin); direct oral anticoagulants are not used for moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis because warfarin was superior in a trial of this population.
  • Symptomatic severe stenosis with favourable anatomy: percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy; otherwise surgical repair or replacement.
  • Pregnancy raises heart rate and plasma volume and can precipitate pulmonary edema; first-line treatment is a β-blocker (such as metoprolol) to lengthen diastolic filling, plus a diuretic for congestion; balloon commissurotomy is an option for refractory symptoms.
A negative throat culture at the time of arthritis does not rule out ARF: by then the infection has usually cleared. Rely on antibody titers and still give penicillin.

s23b-s-080102-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Diagnosis

Complete Kawasaki disease: fever for at least 5 days plus at least 4 of these 5 findings:

  • bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, sparing the limbus;
  • oral changes: red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, diffuse redness of the oral mucosa;
  • a polymorphous rash (not vesicular);
  • extremity changes: red palms and soles with swelling in the acute phase, then peeling around the nails in weeks 2–3;
  • cervical lymphadenopathy, usually one node of 1.5 cm or more and on one side.

Incomplete Kawasaki disease (fewer criteria; common in infants, who are at the highest risk of aneurysm) is diagnosed with supporting labs and echocardiography: raised CRP and ESR, anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis after day 7, low albumin, raised transaminases, sterile pyuria.

Treatment

  • IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion, ideally within the first 10 days of fever (and later if fever or inflammation persists), plus aspirin (moderate or high dose while febrile, then low dose until follow-up echo is normal, typically 6–8 weeks).
  • Echocardiography at diagnosis, at 1–2 weeks and at 4–6 weeks; more often if coronary dilation is found.
  • IVIG resistance (fever 36 hours or more after the infusion): a second IVIG dose, or glucocorticoids or infliximab. Children at high risk of aneurysm may receive glucocorticoids with the first IVIG.
  • Large aneurysms need antithrombotic therapy (low-dose aspirin plus an anticoagulant) and long-term cardiology follow-up for stenosis and ischemia.

Practical points

  • Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) should be delayed about 11 months after IVIG, because passively transferred antibody blunts the response.
  • Children on aspirin need yearly inactivated influenza vaccine (not the live intranasal vaccine), because influenza or varicella during aspirin therapy raises the risk of Reye syndrome.
  • Kawasaki-like features with shock and multisystem involvement after SARS-CoV-2 infection suggest multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), which also affects the coronaries but is more likely to cause myocardial dysfunction and GI symptoms in older children.
Look-alikeDistinguishing feature
Scarlet feverSandpaper rash, exudative pharyngitis, positive rapid strep test; responds to penicillin within a day
MeaslesExudative conjunctivitis, cough and coryza, Koplik spots, rash spreads from the head down
AdenovirusExudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis; lower inflammatory markers
Staphylococcal or streptococcal toxic shockHypotension early, multiorgan failure
Drug reaction (DRESS, Stevens–Johnson)New drug exposure, mucosal erosions, eosinophilia

s23b-s-080102-ck-03.bodyHtml:
Libman–Sacks endocarditis and antiphospholipid syndrome

  • Suspect it in a patient with lupus or antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) who has a new regurgitant murmur or an embolic stroke with negative blood cultures. Echocardiography (often TEE) shows sterile vegetations; test for antiphospholipid antibodies.
  • Patients with APS and thrombosis or embolism need long-term anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin); direct oral anticoagulants performed worse in high-risk (especially triple-positive) APS and are avoided there. Treat active lupus; severe regurgitation may need surgery.

Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis

  • Think of it when a patient with an advanced adenocarcinoma has multiple embolic strokes in different arterial territories and sterile vegetations.
  • Treat with therapeutic heparin (unfractionated or low-molecular-weight), which works better than warfarin in cancer-associated hypercoagulability, and treat the cancer. Rule out infection with blood cultures before labelling vegetations sterile.

Carcinoid heart disease

  • Clues: flushing, diarrhea and wheeze in a patient with a liver mass, plus right-sided heart failure and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur.
  • Best initial test: 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA (or plasma 5-HIAA); avoid serotonin-rich foods (bananas, walnuts, avocado, pineapple) and some drugs before testing. Imaging with somatostatin-receptor PET locates the tumour. Echocardiography stages the heart; NT-proBNP helps screening.
  • Management: somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) control symptoms; telotristat (a tryptophan hydroxylase inhibitor) reduces refractory diarrhea; valve replacement for severe symptomatic disease. Give octreotide around procedures and anesthesia to prevent a carcinoid crisis.

Giant cell arteritis

  • New headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms in someone over 50 with a high ESR or CRP: start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately (IV methylprednisolone if vision is threatened) and arrange temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound within the next 1–2 weeks. Do not delay treatment for the biopsy; steroids do not change the histology quickly.
  • Tocilizumab reduces relapse and steroid exposure. Low-dose aspirin is often added for patients with vascular risk.
  • Because of the risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm, many experts obtain baseline aortic imaging and follow up with periodic imaging.

Takayasu arteritis

  • A young woman with arm claudication, a blood pressure difference of more than 10 mm Hg between arms, weak radial pulses or subclavian bruits.
  • Diagnosis: MR or CT angiography of the aorta and branches (long smooth stenoses, wall thickening); ESR and CRP may be normal despite active disease.
  • Treatment: glucocorticoids with a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, a TNF inhibitor or tocilizumab); revascularisation for critical stenoses once inflammation is controlled. Measure blood pressure in the less-affected limb (or the legs), because the narrowed arm reads falsely low.
In suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms, the wrong answer is "biopsy first". Treat first; one eye can be lost within days and the other soon after.

s23b-s-080101-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Infective endocarditis (IE) is infection of the endocardial surface, usually a heart valve. Its lesion is the vegetation: a friable mass of platelets, fibrin, inflammatory cells and microcolonies of organisms. Organisms in the depth of the vegetation are shielded from neutrophils and are metabolically slow, which is why cure needs weeks of high-dose bactericidal therapy.

How a vegetation starts

  • Damaged endothelium (a jet from regurgitation or stenosis, a prosthetic surface, a catheter) exposes subendothelial matrix. Platelets and fibrin settle there and form a sterile nidus (nonbacterial thrombotic vegetation).
  • Transient bacteremia (chewing, tooth brushing, dental work, injection drug use, intravascular devices, GI or GU procedures) seeds that nidus.
  • Virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus can attach to normal valves directly, using surface adhesins that bind fibronectin and fibrinogen (clumping factor).

Acute versus subacute

Acute IESubacute IE
Typical organismS. aureusViridans group streptococci, enterococci
Valve beforehandOften normalUsually abnormal (prolapse with regurgitation, rheumatic, bicuspid, congenital)
CourseDays; high fever, sepsisWeeks to months; low fever, weight loss, fatigue
VegetationsLarge, destructive; perforation, ring abscessSmaller; less tissue destruction

Organism by clinical setting

SettingOrganism to think of firstPoint to remember
People who inject drugsS. aureus (also streptococci, gram-negative rods, Candida)Tricuspid valve most often; septic pulmonary emboli
Poor dentition or recent dental work, abnormal native valveViridans streptococci (S. sanguinis, S. mutans, S. mitis)Make extracellular dextran (glucan) that sticks to the fibrin–platelet nidus
Older patient, bacteremia from the bowelStreptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I)Strong link with colonic adenoma or carcinoma: colonoscopy
After GU or GI instrumentation, older menEnterococcus faecalisIntrinsically resistant to cephalosporins
Prosthetic valve within months of surgery; devicesCoagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis), S. aureusBiofilm (extracellular polysaccharide) on foreign material
Blood cultures negativePrior antibiotics (commonest); Coxiella burnetii; Bartonella; HACEK; fungiSerology or PCR; HACEK grow slowly
HACEK organisms are fastidious gram-negative bacilli of the mouth and upper airway: Haemophilus (non-influenzae species), Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella. They cause subacute IE with large vegetations.

Culture-negative clues

  • Coxiella burnetii (Q fever): inhaled from dried birth products of cattle, sheep and goats; no arthropod vector needed; an obligate intracellular organism with a hardy spore-like form. Chronic Q fever targets damaged or prosthetic valves.
  • Bartonella quintana: spread by body lice; people experiencing homelessness or alcohol use disorder. Bartonella henselae comes from cats.

Where the clinical signs come from

Fragments of the vegetation embolize (Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages, strokes, splenic and renal infarcts, mycotic aneurysms; septic lung emboli from right-sided disease). Persistent antigenemia drives circulating immune complexes (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, positive rheumatoid factor). Local spread destroys leaflets and invades the annulus: a perivalvular abscess near the aortic root can interrupt the AV node and conducting tissue, so a new PR prolongation or heart block in IE suggests abscess.

Painless versus painful. The painless flat lesions on palms and soles are embolic (Janeway); the painful raised nodules on finger pads are immunologic (Osler). Students mix them up when the stem gives only one adjective.

Valves involved

Left-sided disease dominates overall (mitral slightly more than aortic). Injection drug use shifts infection to the tricuspid valve, which presents with fever, a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that rises with inspiration, and multiple cavitating lung nodules. Right-sided disease has a better prognosis than left-sided disease, partly because systemic emboli are rare.

Bridge to the clinic. Every structural fact above becomes a management rule: organisms inside vegetations need prolonged intravenous bactericidal therapy; abscess and leaflet destruction are surgical problems; S. gallolyticus sends the patient to colonoscopy.

s23b-s-080101-s1-02.bodyHtml:
Beyond bacterial endocarditis, infections reach the heart and aorta through direct viral injury of myocytes, parasitic invasion, spirochetal inflammation of the conduction system and vasculitis of the vasa vasorum.

Viral myocarditis

  • Agents: enteroviruses (classically coxsackievirus B), adenovirus, parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6, influenza and SARS-CoV-2. Coxsackieviruses are picornaviruses: small, nonenveloped, icosahedral, positive-sense single-stranded RNA, spread by the fecal–oral and respiratory routes.
  • Mechanism: direct viral cytopathic injury in the first days, then T-cell–mediated immune injury of myocytes, which can persist after the virus is cleared.
  • Histology: a lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis next to the lymphocytes.
  • Presentation: a young adult with a viral prodrome, then chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmia or heart failure; troponin rises; the ECG may mimic infarction. Most recover; some progress to dilated cardiomyopathy; sudden death can occur in young athletes.

Chagas disease

  • Trypanosoma cruzi, a flagellated protozoan, is transmitted when the feces of a blood-feeding triatomine (reduviid, "kissing") bug contaminate the bite wound or conjunctiva; also by transfusion, transplant, congenitally and by contaminated food. Endemic in rural Mexico, Central and South America.
  • Acute phase: often mild; local swelling at the entry site (unilateral painless eyelid edema when the conjunctiva is the entry point).
  • Chronic phase (decades later): destruction of myocytes and of autonomic ganglion cells. Heart: dilated cardiomyopathy, left ventricular apical aneurysm with mural thrombus, right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block, ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death. Gut: megaesophagus and megacolon.
  • Drugs: benznidazole or nifurtimox (most effective in acute and early chronic infection and in children).

Lyme carditis

  • Borrelia burgdorferi, a spirochete carried by Ixodes ticks (northeastern and upper midwestern US), disseminates weeks after the bite.
  • The classic cardiac lesion is atrioventricular block that can change from minute to minute, from a long PR interval to complete heart block, because inflammation involves the AV node.
  • It usually resolves with antibiotics, so a permanent pacemaker is rarely needed.

Syphilitic (luetic) aortitis

  • A manifestation of tertiary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) appearing 10–30 years after infection.
  • Mechanism: obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta → ischemic loss of medial smooth muscle and elastic fibres → scarring that wrinkles the intima ("tree-bark" appearance).
  • Results: aneurysm of the ascending aorta and arch, dilation of the aortic root with aortic regurgitation, and narrowing of the coronary ostia. Calcification of the ascending aorta on a chest film is a clue.

s23b-s-080102-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is a delayed, nonsuppurative, immune-mediated inflammatory disease that follows pharyngitis caused by group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes). It affects mostly children aged 5–15 years in low-resource settings and in some Indigenous communities. Its lasting harm is rheumatic heart disease (RHD), still a leading cause of acquired heart disease in young people worldwide.

Pathogenesis: molecular mimicry

  • Antibodies and T cells raised against the streptococcal M protein (and the N-acetylglucosamine of the cell wall) cross-react with host proteins: cardiac myosin, tropomyosin, laminin of valve endothelium, and neuronal antigens of the basal ganglia (chorea). This is a type II hypersensitivity reaction, with a T-cell component in the valve.
  • Only throat infection triggers ARF. Skin infection (impetigo) can cause post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever.
  • Host susceptibility matters: only a small share of untreated pharyngitis episodes lead to ARF, and recurrences cluster in people who have had it before.

Pathology: a pancarditis

  • Aschoff bodies: foci of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, plasma cells and plump macrophages called Anitschkow cells, whose nuclei hold a central wavy ribbon of chromatin ("caterpillar" nuclei). Some fuse into multinucleated Aschoff giant cells.
  • Myocarditis causes heart failure and is the usual cause of death in the acute phase.
  • Endocarditis/valvulitis: small, warty, sterile vegetations along the lines of leaflet closure (the mitral valve most often, then the aortic).
  • Pericarditis: fibrinous ("bread and butter"), usually resolving without constriction.

Clinical features

Major manifestationsWhat to know
CarditisNew mitral regurgitation murmur (acute), aortic regurgitation, pericardial rub, heart failure; may be subclinical and seen only on echo
ArthritisMigratory polyarthritis of large joints, very responsive to aspirin or NSAIDs, leaves no deformity
Sydenham choreaRapid, purposeless movements and emotional lability; appears 1–8 months after the infection; can be the only finding
Erythema marginatumEvanescent pink rings with pale centres on the trunk
Subcutaneous nodulesPainless, firm, over bony prominences and tendons; travel with carditis

Minor findings are fever, arthralgia, raised ESR or CRP, and a prolonged PR interval. The diagnosis (revised Jones criteria) combines manifestations with evidence of recent group A streptococcal infection: a rising or raised antistreptolysin O or anti-DNase B titer, or a positive throat culture or rapid antigen test.

Chronic rheumatic heart disease

  • Repeated or severe episodes heal by fibrosis and neovascularisation: leaflets thicken and calcify, commissures fuse and chordae shorten and fuse.
  • Mitral stenosis is the signature lesion ("fish-mouth" orifice), often with regurgitation; the aortic valve is next; tricuspid involvement nearly always accompanies mitral disease; the pulmonic valve is rarely affected.
  • Consequences: left atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, left atrial thrombus and stroke, pulmonary hypertension, and higher risk of infective endocarditis.
Acute versus chronic valve lesion. In acute rheumatic fever the new murmur is usually mitral regurgitation (valvulitis). Mitral stenosis is the scarred, chronic result years later. Pregnancy often unmasks it, because higher heart rate and volume raise left atrial pressure.
Why prophylaxis works. Each new streptococcal pharyngitis can restart the cross-reactive response and add valve damage, so preventing reinfection (long-acting penicillin) prevents progression.

Not every vegetation is infected. Three sterile valve lesions are tested by comparing their size, position and cause.

Rheumatic vegetationsLibman–Sacks endocarditisNonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)Infective endocarditis
CauseImmune response after group A strep pharyngitisSystemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndromeHypercoagulable states, especially mucin-producing adenocarcinoma; severe chronic illnessBacteria or fungi
Size and lookSmall, warty, in a rowSmall to medium, flat or verrucousSmall, bland, loosely attachedLarge, friable, destructive
PositionLines of closureBoth surfaces of the leaflet, and chordaeLines of closureAnywhere; often the upstream surface
Main riskLater scarring (stenosis)Regurgitation, embolic strokeSystemic emboli (stroke, infarcts)Destruction, emboli, sepsis

Libman–Sacks endocarditis

  • Sterile vegetations of fibrin, immune complexes and mononuclear cells, most often on the mitral valve, on the atrial and ventricular faces alike.
  • Strongly associated with antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I). It causes mitral regurgitation and cerebral emboli more than stenosis.

Nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis

  • Small sterile thrombi on otherwise normal valves in a hypercoagulable patient. The classic setting is a mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma (pancreas, lung, stomach, ovary), where mucin and tissue factor activate coagulation (the same process causes migratory thrombophlebitis).
  • Presents with embolic stroke or infarcts of spleen, kidney or limbs; blood cultures are negative.

Carcinoid heart disease

  • Occurs when a well-differentiated neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumour, usually of the small intestine, has spread to the liver, so that serotonin and other vasoactive products reach the systemic veins without first-pass hepatic breakdown.
  • Serotonin stimulates fibroblasts: plaque-like deposits of fibrous tissue form on the endocardium of the right heart, thickening and fixing the tricuspid and pulmonic valves → tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonic stenosis or regurgitation.
  • The left heart is spared because monoamine oxidase in the lung degrades serotonin. Left-sided lesions point to a bronchial carcinoid, a right-to-left shunt (such as a patent foramen ovale) or very high hormone levels.
  • The carcinoid syndrome: flushing, watery diarrhea, wheeze, and right-sided heart failure. Serotonin is metabolised to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), which is measured in the urine. Heavy use of tryptophan for serotonin can cause niacin deficiency (pellagra).
Drugs that act on the serotonin 5-HT2B receptor (the old appetite suppressant fenfluramine, ergot-derived dopamine agonists such as pergolide and cabergoline at high doses) can produce a similar fibrotic valvulopathy.

s23b-s-080102-s1-03.bodyHtml:
Three vasculitides are tested for their cardiac or aortic damage. They are sorted by the size of vessel they attack and by the patient's age.

Kawasaki diseaseTakayasu arteritisGiant cell arteritis
Vessel sizeMedium (coronary arteries)Large (aorta and its branches)Large and medium (branches of the carotid, aorta)
Typical patientChild under 5 years, more often of East Asian ancestryWoman under 40 years, more often of Asian ancestryAdult over 50 years
HistologyTransmural necrotising inflammation, then fibrosisGranulomatous inflammation of media and adventitia, with intimal thickeningGranulomatous inflammation with giant cells, fragmented internal elastic lamina
Cardiovascular resultCoronary artery aneurysm, thrombosis, MIStenosis of arch branches: weak arm pulses, unequal blood pressures, bruits, renal artery stenosis, aortic regurgitationThoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection years later; arm claudication

Kawasaki disease

  • An acute, self-limited vasculitis of young children with prolonged fever and mucocutaneous inflammation: bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, red cracked lips and "strawberry" tongue, polymorphous rash, swollen red hands and feet followed by peeling of the fingertips, and cervical lymph node enlargement.
  • The cause is unknown; an infectious trigger in genetically susceptible children is suspected. Activated immune cells injure the coronary artery wall, which can dilate into aneurysms.
  • Untreated, about a quarter of children develop coronary aneurysms; prompt intravenous immunoglobulin lowers that risk to a few per cent. It is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in high-income countries.

Takayasu arteritis

  • Starts with fever, malaise and arthralgia, then signs of narrowed arch vessels ("pulseless disease"): arm claudication, a systolic pressure difference between the arms, absent radial pulses, visual and neurologic symptoms.
  • Aortic root dilation can cause aortic regurgitation; renal artery stenosis causes hypertension.

Giant cell (temporal) arteritis

  • Headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual loss in an older adult, often with polymyalgia rheumatica; ESR and CRP are high.
  • The cytokine IL-6 drives the systemic inflammation; tocilizumab, a monoclonal antibody against the IL-6 receptor, spares glucocorticoids.
  • Involvement of the aorta raises the long-term risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm.

Immune pericarditis after cardiac injury

Post-MI pericarditis (Dressler syndrome) and post-pericardiotomy syndrome appear weeks after injury: fever, pleuritic chest pain, a rub and effusion. Antibodies against myocardial antigens released by the injury are thought to cause them. Details are in the pericardium chapter.

Do not confuse Kawasaki with polyarteritis nodosa: both hit medium arteries, but PAN affects adults (renal, mesenteric, nerve), is linked with hepatitis B and spares the lungs; Kawasaki is a childhood disease of the coronaries.

s23b-s-080201-ck-01.bodyHtml:
When to suspect a cardiac mass

  • Embolic stroke, retinal artery occlusion or acute limb ischemia in a patient in sinus rhythm, especially if young.
  • Dyspnea, orthopnea or syncope that varies with posture, with a diastolic murmur or early diastolic sound but no history of rheumatic fever.
  • Unexplained fever, weight loss, anemia and high ESR/CRP with negative blood cultures.
  • A known cancer with new pericardial effusion, arrhythmia, heart block or heart failure.

Imaging

TestRole
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)Best initial test for any suspected intracardiac mass; shows size, attachment, mobility and valve obstruction
Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE)Better for small masses, the atria and appendage, valve-based lesions and the attachment point
Cardiac MRITissue characterization (fat, fibrous tissue, vascularity, thrombus vs tumor), extent, planning
CT (cardiac or chest/abdomen/pelvis), PETExtracardiac extent, staging, search for a primary cancer

Differential diagnosis of a left atrial mass: myxoma (stalk on the septum, mobile), thrombus (left atrial appendage, atrial fibrillation or mitral stenosis, immobile, shrinks with anticoagulation), vegetation (valve leaflet, positive cultures, fever) and sarcoma (broad base, invasive).

Management by lesion

  • Myxoma: surgical excision soon after diagnosis, because of the risk of embolism and sudden obstruction. The stalk and a cuff of the septum are removed to reduce recurrence. Anticoagulation does not treat the tumor. After excision, follow with periodic echocardiography; recurrence is uncommon after a sporadic myxoma and more likely in familial disease.
  • Carney complex: suspect it with multiple, recurrent or unusual-site myxomas, a young patient, skin pigmentation or endocrine tumors. Offer genetic counselling, PRKAR1A testing and screening of first-degree relatives (including echocardiography), plus lifelong surveillance for new cardiac and endocrine tumors.
  • Papillary fibroelastoma: excision for a lesion that has embolized, is mobile or is large; small, immobile, asymptomatic lesions may be followed.
  • Rhabdomyoma (child): usually observation with serial echocardiography because most regress. Treat when there is hemodynamically important obstruction or refractory arrhythmia (surgery, or an mTOR inhibitor in selected cases). Evaluate the child for tuberous sclerosis.
  • Angiosarcoma and other sarcomas: multidisciplinary care; resection when feasible, with chemotherapy and radiotherapy; the prognosis is poor.
  • Metastatic disease: treat the cancer; manage the complications.

Malignant pericardial effusion

Suspect tamponade with dyspnea, hypotension, tachycardia, raised jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus; the ECG may show low voltage and electrical alternans. Echocardiography confirms the effusion and shows chamber collapse. Hemodynamic compromise needs urgent pericardiocentesis (send fluid for cytology). Malignant effusions often recur, so definitive options include extended catheter drainage, a surgical pericardial window, or intrapericardial sclerosis in selected patients, together with systemic cancer treatment.

Exam trap: a left atrial mass in a patient with atrial fibrillation and mitral stenosis is a thrombus until proven otherwise; a pedunculated septal mass in a patient in sinus rhythm is a myxoma. Do not answer "anticoagulate and repeat the echo" for a myxoma.
High yield: constitutional symptoms and inflammatory labs of myxoma resolve after excision; persistent or recurrent symptoms suggest recurrence.

s23b-s-080201-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Tumors of the heart are rare, and the first rule is about proportions: a mass found in or on the heart of an adult is far more often a metastasis than a primary tumor. Among primary tumors, most are benign, and the benign tumors that matter for the exam are the myxoma (adults), the rhabdomyoma (infants and children), the papillary fibroelastoma (valves of older adults) and the lipoma. The most common primary malignant tumor in adults is angiosarcoma.

Myxoma

Where and what. About three quarters arise in the left atrium, typically on a stalk attached to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis; most of the rest are in the right atrium. Grossly the tumor is soft, gelatinous and lobulated, sometimes friable and villous. Microscopically, scattered stellate and spindle-shaped "myxoma cells", single or in cords and ring-like clusters around small vessels, sit in an abundant mucopolysaccharide (myxoid) ground substance, often with hemorrhage and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. The cells are thought to derive from multipotent subendocardial mesenchyme.

How it causes disease. Three mechanisms explain almost every presentation:

  • Obstruction. A mobile pedunculated mass prolapses into the mitral orifice in diastole, acting like a ball valve. Symptoms mimic mitral stenosis (dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary edema) but characteristically change with body position; sudden obstruction can cause presyncope or syncope. A low-pitched early diastolic sound as the tumor hits the ventricle (the "plop") may be heard, along with a diastolic rumble. Right atrial myxomas obstruct the tricuspid valve and mimic right heart failure.
  • Embolism. Fragments of a friable left-sided tumor embolize to the systemic circulation (brain, retina, limbs, kidneys); right-sided tumors embolize to the pulmonary arteries. A young patient in sinus rhythm with an embolic stroke should prompt echocardiography.
  • Constitutional effects. Myxomas secrete interleukin-6, which drives fever, weight loss, fatigue, arthralgia, anemia, raised ESR and CRP and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The picture can be mistaken for endocarditis, vasculitis or a connective tissue disease; it resolves after excision.

Familial disease. About 5–10% of myxomas are familial, most within Carney complex: autosomal dominant, usually from loss-of-function variants in PRKAR1A, which encodes the type 1A regulatory subunit of protein kinase A (so cAMP signalling is unrestrained). Features: myxomas of the heart (often multiple, unusual sites, younger patients, recurrent), skin and breast; spotty pigmentation (lentigines, blue nevi) of the face, lips and conjunctiva; and endocrine overactivity such as primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome), GH-secreting pituitary adenoma, testicular tumors and thyroid nodules.

Pattern to recognise: young or middle-aged adult, sinus rhythm, positional dyspnea or syncope, a diastolic sound, embolic event and "inflammatory" labs. Think left atrial myxoma before rheumatic mitral stenosis.

Rhabdomyoma

The most common primary cardiac tumor of infants and children. Usually multiple, within the ventricular walls or septum, and strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC1 hamartin, TSC2 tuberin; loss of either removes inhibition of mTOR signalling). Histology shows enlarged, vacuolated, glycogen-rich myocytes in which strands of cytoplasm radiate from the nucleus to the membrane ("spider cells"). Rhabdomyomas are hamartomas: they often appear in fetal life and regress spontaneously during infancy. They can cause arrhythmias (including pre-excitation) or outflow obstruction.

Other primary tumors

TumorTypical patient and siteKey features
Papillary fibroelastomaOlder adults; valve surfaces, most often aortic then mitralSmall, mobile, frond-like avascular papillae with an elastic core lined by endothelium; usually incidental but can cause embolic stroke or TIA
LipomaAdults; subendocardial or interatrial septumMature fat; lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum is a related non-neoplastic finding that spares the fossa ovalis
FibromaChildren; ventricular myocardiumSolitary, can cause ventricular arrhythmia; associated with Gorlin (nevoid basal cell carcinoma) syndrome
AngiosarcomaAdults; most often the right atriumMalignant endothelial cells (CD31, ERG positive) forming irregular vascular channels; hemorrhagic pericardial effusion, tamponade, early metastasis; poor prognosis

Metastases to the heart

Secondary tumors outnumber primaries many times over at autopsy. In absolute numbers the most frequent sources are the common cancers that reach the mediastinum: lung and breast carcinoma, and lymphoma/leukemia. Relative to how often each cancer occurs, melanoma has the highest rate of cardiac involvement. Routes are direct invasion (lung, esophagus), lymphatic spread (pericardium), hematogenous spread (myocardium) and intracavitary extension along the vena cava (renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma).

The pericardium is the most commonly involved layer: a malignant, often hemorrhagic, effusion that may cause tamponade. Myocardial deposits cause arrhythmias, conduction block or heart failure.

Exam trap: "most common cardiac tumor" without a qualifier is a metastasis; "most common primary cardiac tumor in adults" is myxoma; "in children" is rhabdomyoma; "most common primary malignant" is angiosarcoma in adults.
Bridge: the IL-6 of a myxoma is the same cytokine that drives hepatic acute-phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, hepcidin), which is why the anemia looks like anemia of inflammation.

s23b-s-080301-ck-01.bodyHtml:
First question: is the patient stable?

A tachycardia is unstable when it causes hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest pain or acute heart failure. Any unstable tachycardia with a pulse is treated with synchronized cardioversion, whatever the rhythm, after sedation if time allows. A pulseless rhythm is cardiac arrest (see the cardiac arrest section). Only when the patient is stable do you work through the ECG.

Stable tachycardia: narrow or wide, regular or irregular

RegularIrregular
Narrow (QRS < 0.12 s)Sinus tachycardia (treat the cause), paroxysmal SVT (AVNRT, AVRT), atrial flutter with fixed conduction, focal atrial tachycardiaAtrial fibrillation, flutter with variable conduction, multifocal atrial tachycardia (three or more P-wave shapes, often with COPD or other severe lung disease)
Wide (QRS ≥ 0.12 s)Ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise; SVT with aberrancy is less likely, especially with structural heart diseaseAF with bundle branch block, pre-excited AF (WPW), polymorphic VT/torsades

Paroxysmal SVT

Typical patient: young and otherwise well, with sudden-onset regular palpitations at 150–250/min that stop abruptly. Steps: vagal maneuvers (modified Valsalva, carotid sinus massage if no bruit or cerebrovascular disease) → IV adenosine (rapid push, then a flush; a larger second dose if needed) → IV diltiazem/verapamil or a β-blocker → synchronized cardioversion if all fail or the patient becomes unstable. Recurrent episodes: catheter ablation is curative and generally preferred over long-term drugs.

Atrial fibrillation and flutter

AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia; risk rises with age, hypertension, obesity, sleep apnea, alcohol, valvular disease, heart failure and hyperthyroidism (check TSH at diagnosis). Management has four parts:

  1. Stability: unstable → synchronized cardioversion.
  2. Stroke prevention: estimate risk with CHA2DS2-VASc (congestive heart failure 1, hypertension 1, age ≥ 75 years 2, diabetes 1, prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism 2, vascular disease 1, age 65–74 years 1, female sex 1). Oral anticoagulation is recommended at a score of 2 or more in men or 3 or more in women and reasonable at 1 in men or 2 in women. European guidance now uses the same score without the sex point. A direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) is preferred over warfarin, except with a mechanical heart valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, where warfarin is required. Aspirin alone is not adequate stroke prevention. Left atrial appendage occlusion is an option when long-term anticoagulation is contraindicated. Atrial flutter is anticoagulated the same way.
  3. Rate control: β-blocker or diltiazem/verapamil (avoid nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction); digoxin is an add-on, especially in heart failure or low blood pressure. A resting target below about 100–110/min is acceptable if symptoms are controlled.
  4. Rhythm control: for persistent symptoms, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, difficult rate control, or early in the disease course. Options include cardioversion, antiarrhythmics chosen by heart structure (flecainide or propafenone only without structural or ischemic heart disease; amiodarone or dofetilide with heart failure; sotalol or dronedarone in selected patients) and catheter ablation, which is increasingly first-line for symptomatic paroxysmal AF and for AF with reduced ejection fraction.
Before elective cardioversion of AF lasting 48 hours or longer (or of unknown duration), either anticoagulate for at least 3 weeks or exclude left atrial thrombus with transesophageal echocardiography. Anticoagulate for at least 4 weeks afterwards regardless of the risk score, then decide long-term therapy by the score.

Also treat contributors: weight loss, alcohol reduction, treatment of sleep apnea and blood pressure control all lower AF burden.

Wide-complex tachycardia

Treat a stable regular wide-complex tachycardia as VT, especially in an older patient with prior infarction or heart failure. Options are IV amiodarone, IV procainamide (avoid in heart failure or a long QT) or elective synchronized cardioversion. Adenosine is used only if the rhythm is regular and monomorphic and SVT with aberrancy is likely. Never give a calcium channel blocker for an undiagnosed wide-complex tachycardia: it can cause collapse if the rhythm is VT.

Pre-excited atrial fibrillation (WPW)

Very fast, irregular, wide QRS complexes that vary in shape. Unstable → synchronized cardioversion. Stable → IV procainamide or ibutilide. Avoid AV nodal blockers (adenosine, β-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin; IV amiodarone is also best avoided) because they can speed conduction down the pathway and precipitate ventricular fibrillation. Definitive therapy is catheter ablation of the pathway.

Torsades de pointes

Polymorphic VT with a long QT on the preceding sinus beats. Give IV magnesium sulfate; stop all QT-prolonging drugs; correct potassium and magnesium. If the episodes are pause-dependent and recur, increasing the heart rate (temporary overdrive pacing or isoproterenol) shortens the QT. If the patient is pulseless, defibrillate.

Premature beats

Isolated premature atrial or ventricular contractions are common and usually benign. Look for triggers (caffeine, alcohol, stimulants, low potassium or magnesium, thyroid disease) and structural heart disease (echocardiogram). A very high premature ventricular contraction burden (roughly over 10–15% of beats on ambulatory monitoring) can cause a reversible cardiomyopathy; symptomatic or high-burden ectopy is treated with a β-blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, or with ablation.

s23b-s-080301-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Approach

A slow heart rate matters when it causes symptoms (syncope, presyncope, fatigue, exertional intolerance, heart failure) or when the rhythm is one that can suddenly worsen. Always look for reversible causes before committing to a permanent pacemaker: AV nodal blocking drugs (β-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin, amiodarone), hyperkalemia, hypothyroidism, acute inferior myocardial infarction, increased vagal tone, Lyme carditis, and obstructive sleep apnea.

Acute symptomatic bradycardia

  1. Assess airway, breathing and circulation; attach monitor; obtain a 12-lead ECG and IV access.
  2. If there are signs of poor perfusion: atropine IV, repeated as needed up to the maximum dose.
  3. If atropine fails: transcutaneous pacing or an infusion of dopamine or epinephrine, then expert consultation for transvenous pacing.
Atropine works on the sinus and AV nodes. In Mobitz II or complete heart block with a wide escape rhythm (block below the node), it rarely helps; go to pacing without delay. In a heart transplant recipient, the denervated heart does not respond to atropine.

Which conduction problems need a permanent pacemaker?

FindingUsual coursePacing
First-degree AV blockBenignNo (unless very long PR with symptoms)
Mobitz IUsually benign, nodalOnly if clearly symptomatic and no reversible cause
Mobitz II, advanced (high-grade) or third-degree AV blockCan progress to asystoleYes, when not due to a reversible cause, even without symptoms
Sinus node dysfunctionEpisodic pauses, chronotropic incompetence, tachy–brady syndromeYes, when symptoms correlate with bradycardia
Alternating left and right bundle branch blockDiffuse infranodal diseaseYes

Sick sinus syndrome

Degenerative fibrosis of the sinus node in older adults causes sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses or arrest, and, in the tachy–brady form, alternation with atrial fibrillation or flutter. Diagnosis is by correlating symptoms with the rhythm on ambulatory monitoring (Holter for daily symptoms, event or implantable loop recorder for rarer ones). Treatment is a pacemaker, which also makes it safe to give the rate-controlling drugs that the tachycardia episodes need.

Carotid sinus hypersensitivity

An exaggerated baroreflex: pressure on the carotid sinus (tight collar, shaving, turning the head) causes a pause of 3 seconds or more (cardioinhibitory type), a fall in systolic pressure of 50 mm Hg or more (vasodepressor type), or both. It mainly affects older men and causes falls and syncope. Diagnose with carotid sinus massage under monitoring (not in patients with a carotid bruit or recent stroke/TIA). Recurrent syncope from the cardioinhibitory type is treated with dual-chamber pacing.

Bundle branch blocks

  • Right bundle branch block: QRS ≥ 0.12 s, rsR′ ("M-shaped") complex in V1, wide slurred S wave in I and V6. Can be normal; new RBBB may signal pulmonary embolism or right heart strain.
  • Left bundle branch block: QRS ≥ 0.12 s, broad notched R in I, aVL and V6, deep S in V1. Almost always reflects structural heart disease; echocardiography is warranted. It distorts ST segments, so ischemia is judged with specific criteria, and a suspected infarction with LBBB and hemodynamic instability or ongoing ischemia goes to urgent angiography. LBBB with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction is the main indication for cardiac resynchronization therapy.

Pacemaker malfunction

ProblemECGCommon causes
Failure to capturePacing spikes not followed by a P wave or QRSLead dislodgement (especially in the first weeks), lead fracture, rising threshold (fibrosis, hyperkalemia, antiarrhythmic drugs), battery depletion
Failure to sense (undersensing)Pacing spikes appear inappropriately soon after, or on top of, the patient's own complexesLead problems, low intrinsic signal, programming
OversensingPauses with no pacing because the device mistakes noise (muscle potentials, electromagnetic interference) for heartbeatsMyopotentials, lead fracture, interference
Failure to pace (output failure)No spikes despite bradycardiaBattery depletion, lead fracture, oversensing

Initial work-up: 12-lead ECG, chest radiograph (lead position and integrity), electrolytes, and device interrogation. Placing a magnet over a pacemaker switches it to asynchronous pacing at a fixed rate, which is useful during surgery with electrocautery or when oversensing is suspected.

s23b-s-080301-ck-03.bodyHtml:
Adult cardiac arrest

Recognize arrest (unresponsive, not breathing normally, no definite pulse within 10 seconds), call for help and a defibrillator, and start high-quality chest compressions: a rate of 100–120/min, a depth of at least 5 cm, full recoil, minimal interruptions, and a compression-to-ventilation ratio of 30:2 until an advanced airway is placed.

Shockable: ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VTNonshockable: pulseless electrical activity, asystole
First actionDefibrillate (unsynchronized) as soon as possible, then resume CPR immediately for 2 minutesCPR; give epinephrine as soon as possible
EpinephrineAfter the second shock, then every 3–5 minutesEvery 3–5 minutes
AntiarrhythmicAmiodarone (or lidocaine) after the third shock for refractory VF/pulseless VTNone
Key additional stepCheck rhythm every 2 minutesSearch for and treat reversible causes

Reversible causes to check in every arrest: hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo- or hyperkalemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis (pulmonary embolism or coronary). Treat each specifically, for example calcium for hyperkalemia, needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, pericardiocentesis for tamponade, thrombolysis for suspected massive pulmonary embolism. Quantitative waveform capnography confirms tube placement and tracks CPR quality; a sudden sustained rise in end-tidal CO2 suggests return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC).

Synchronized cardioversion is for organized tachycardias with a pulse. A pulseless patient in VF or VT gets unsynchronized defibrillation: the device cannot synchronize to a chaotic rhythm and waiting for it wastes time.

After return of spontaneous circulation

  • Support oxygenation (avoid both hypoxemia and excessive oxygen) and blood pressure (avoid hypotension; aim for a mean arterial pressure of at least about 65 mm Hg).
  • Obtain a 12-lead ECG. ST elevation → emergent coronary angiography. Without ST elevation, urgent angiography is decided case by case.
  • For patients who remain comatose, use deliberate temperature control and prevent fever.
  • Delay neurologic prognostication until at least 72 hours after normothermia, using several modalities.

Sudden cardiac death and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators

Most sudden cardiac death in adults comes from ventricular arrhythmias in ischemic heart disease. In the young, think of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, inherited channelopathies (long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT), arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, anomalous coronary arteries, myocarditis, WPW and commotio cordis.

  • Secondary prevention: an ICD after survived VF or sustained hemodynamically unstable VT without a completely reversible cause.
  • Primary prevention: an ICD for left ventricular ejection fraction ≤ 35% with NYHA class II–III symptoms despite at least 3 months of optimal medical therapy (and at least 40 days after a myocardial infarction), with reasonable expected survival.

Congenital long QT syndrome in practice

Suspect it with syncope during exercise, swimming, startle or sleep, a family history of sudden death or drowning, or a long QT found incidentally. Management: avoid QT-prolonging drugs, keep potassium and magnesium normal, give a β-blocker (nonselective agents such as nadolol or propranolol are preferred), screen first-degree relatives with ECGs and genetic testing, and place an ICD after cardiac arrest or with recurrent events despite therapy.

Acquired long QT

Common culprits: class IA and III antiarrhythmics, macrolides and fluoroquinolones, azole antifungals, methadone, ondansetron, haloperidol and other antipsychotics, citalopram and tricyclic antidepressants, plus hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypocalcemia. Risk is highest with several drugs combined, bradycardia, female sex, heart disease and older age. Check a baseline ECG before starting a QT-prolonging drug in at-risk patients.

to check in every arrest: hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo- or hyperkalemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis (pulmonary embolism or coronary). Treat each specifically, for example calcium for hyperkalemia, needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, pericardiocentesis for tamponade, thrombolysis for suspected massive pulmonary embolism. Quantitative waveform capnography confirms tube placement and tracks CPR quality; a sudden sustained rise in end-tidal CO

Synchronized cardioversion is for organized tachycardias with a pulse. A pulseless patient in VF or VT gets unsynchronized defibrillation: the device cannot synchronize to a chaotic rhythm and waiting for it wastes time.
Support oxygenation (avoid both hypoxemia and excessive oxygen) and blood pressure (avoid hypotension; aim for a mean arterial pressure of at least about 65 mm Hg).
. Without ST elevation, urgent angiography is decided case by case.
For patients who remain comatose, use deliberate temperature control and prevent fever.
Delay neurologic prognostication until at least 72 hours after normothermia, using several modalities.
Sudden cardiac death and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators

Most sudden cardiac death in adults comes from ventricular arrhythmias in ischemic heart disease. In the young, think of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, inherited channelopathies (long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT), arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, anomalous coronary arteries, myocarditis, WPW and commotio cordis.
: an ICD after survived VF or sustained hemodynamically unstable VT without a completely reversible cause.

: an ICD for left ventricular ejection fraction ≤ 35% with NYHA class II–III symptoms despite at least 3 months of optimal medical therapy (and at least 40 days after a myocardial infarction), with reasonable expected survival.
Congenital long QT syndrome in practice

Suspect it with syncope during exercise, swimming, startle or sleep, a family history of sudden death or drowning, or a long QT found incidentally. Management: avoid QT-prolonging drugs, keep potassium and magnesium normal, give a β-blocker (nonselective agents such as nadolol or propranolol are preferred), screen first-degree relatives with ECGs and genetic testing, and place an ICD after cardiac arrest or with recurrent events despite therapy.

Common culprits: class IA and III antiarrhythmics, macrolides and fluoroquinolones, azole antifungals, methadone, ondansetron, haloperidol and other antipsychotics, citalopram and tricyclic antidepressants, plus hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypocalcemia. Risk is highest with several drugs combined, bradycardia, female sex, heart disease and older age. Check a baseline ECG before starting a QT-prolonging drug in at-risk patients.

s23b-s-080301-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Every heartbeat starts as a wave of depolarization that the conduction system delivers in a fixed order: sinoatrial (SA) node → atrial myocardium → atrioventricular (AV) node → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricular myocardium. Arrhythmias are failures of this order: impulses that start in the wrong place (abnormal automaticity or triggered activity), travel in a circle (re-entry) or fail to travel (block).

Two kinds of action potential

PhaseVentricular myocyte and Purkinje fibre (fast response)SA and AV nodal cell (slow response)
4Stable resting potential near −85 to −90 mV, held by the inward-rectifier K+ current (IK1)Spontaneous diastolic depolarization: the "funny" current If through HCN channels (mostly Na+ in), then T-type Ca2+ current
0Rapid upstroke from voltage-gated Na+ channels (INa)Slow upstroke carried by L-type Ca2+ channels
1Early partial repolarization: Na+ channels inactivate, transient outward K+ current (Ito)Absent
2Plateau: L-type Ca2+ influx balanced by delayed-rectifier K+ efflux; the Ca2+ entering triggers Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (excitation–contraction coupling)Absent
3Repolarization by the rapid (IKr, hERG) and slow (IKs) delayed-rectifier K+ currentsRepolarization by K+ efflux

The slope of phase 4 in the SA node sets the heart rate. Sympathetic stimulation (β1 receptors → cAMP) steepens it by increasing If and Ca2+ currents. Vagal stimulation (M2 receptors) flattens it and hyperpolarizes the cell by opening acetylcholine-activated K+ channels. Ivabradine blocks If directly and slows the sinus rate without changing contractility or blood pressure.

The fast-response cells depend on Na+ channels for their upstroke; the nodal cells depend on Ca2+ channels. That is why class I drugs mainly slow conduction in myocardium and Purkinje tissue (wider QRS) while β-blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers mainly slow the AV node (longer PR).

Conduction velocity and refractoriness

Conduction is fastest in Purkinje fibres, slower in atrial and ventricular muscle and slowest in the AV node. The AV node's delay (most of the PR interval) gives the atria time to finish filling the ventricles and, because the node's refractory period lengthens at high rates, it protects the ventricles from very fast atrial rhythms. An accessory pathway that bypasses the node removes this protection.

During the effective refractory period (phase 0 to late phase 3) a new stimulus cannot produce a propagated action potential. A stimulus in the relative refractory period, which overlaps the downslope of the T wave, can; this is the vulnerable window in which an early impulse ("R on T") can start ventricular fibrillation.

Reading the ECG intervals

IntervalNormalWhat it measuresProlonged by
PR0.12–0.20 sAtrial depolarization plus AV nodal delayAV nodal disease, β-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, high vagal tone
QRS< 0.12 sVentricular depolarizationBundle branch block, class IA/IC drugs, hyperkalemia, tricyclic overdose, ventricular origin of the beat
QT (corrected for rate)roughly ≤ 0.44 s in men, ≤ 0.46 s in womenDepolarization plus repolarizationClass IA and III drugs, many antimicrobials and antipsychotics, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, congenital channel defects

Blood supply of the conduction system

The SA node is usually supplied by the right coronary artery (about 60% of people) and the AV node by the artery that gives off the posterior descending artery, most often the right coronary artery. This is why inferior myocardial infarction is often accompanied by sinus bradycardia and AV nodal block (usually transient), while anterior infarction that damages the bundle branches tends to cause infranodal block with a worse outlook.

Step 1 to clinic: knowing whether a block sits in the AV node (narrow escape, responds to atropine, often transient) or below it (wide escape, unreliable, needs pacing) predicts both its danger and its treatment.

Antiarrhythmics are grouped by the main current or receptor they act on (the Vaughan Williams classes). Many drugs have actions in more than one class, so learn each drug's dominant effect and its signature toxicity.

ClassMain actionECG effectExamplesSignature adverse effects
IAModerate Na+ channel block plus K+ channel block: slower phase 0, longer action potentialQRS and QT longerProcainamide, quinidine, disopyramideTorsades de pointes; procainamide: drug-induced lupus (positive antihistone antibodies), agranulocytosis; quinidine: cinchonism (tinnitus, headache), diarrhea; disopyramide: anticholinergic effects, negative inotropy
IBWeak, rapidly dissociating Na+ block that favours depolarized (ischemic) tissue; shortens the action potentialLittle changeLidocaine, mexiletineCNS toxicity: perioral numbness, tremor, confusion, seizures
ICStrong, slowly dissociating Na+ block; marked use dependence (more block at faster rates); action potential duration unchangedQRS much longerFlecainide, propafenoneProarrhythmia and excess mortality in structural heart disease and after myocardial infarction; can convert AF to slow flutter with 1:1 AV conduction, so an AV nodal blocker is given with it
IIβ1 blockade: flatter phase 4 in the nodes, slower AV conductionPR longerMetoprolol, esmolol, propranololBradycardia, AV block, bronchospasm with nonselective agents, fatigue, masking of hypoglycemia
IIIK+ channel (IKr) block: longer phase 3 and refractory periodQT longerAmiodarone, dronedarone, sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilideTorsades (sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide: start in hospital with QT and renal monitoring); amiodarone: see below
IVL-type Ca2+ channel block in nodal tissuePR longerVerapamil, diltiazemBradycardia, AV block, hypotension, constipation (verapamil), worsening of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

Amiodarone

Amiodarone has class I, II, III and IV actions. Although it prolongs the QT interval, it causes torsades less often than other class III drugs because it prolongs refractoriness evenly. Its toxicity comes from iodine content, lipophilicity and a very long half-life: pulmonary fibrosis or pneumonitis, hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, raised transaminases, corneal microdeposits, optic neuropathy, photosensitivity and blue-grey skin, and bradycardia. It inhibits several cytochrome P450 enzymes and P-glycoprotein, raising warfarin and digoxin levels. Baseline and periodic thyroid and liver tests, plus a baseline chest radiograph and attention to new cough or dyspnea, are standard.

Drugs outside the classes

  • Adenosine acts on A1 receptors in the AV node, increasing K+ conductance and reducing Ca2+ current, which causes a transient (seconds-long) AV block. It terminates re-entry that uses the AV node and unmasks flutter waves in atrial flutter. Expected effects: flushing, chest discomfort, dyspnea and a brief pause. Methylxanthines (theophylline, caffeine) block adenosine receptors and blunt its effect; dipyridamole blocks its uptake and enhances it.
  • Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase (positive inotropy) and raises vagal tone (slower AV conduction).
  • Magnesium sulfate suppresses the early afterdepolarizations that trigger torsades de pointes, even when serum magnesium is normal.
  • Ivabradine blocks If in the SA node; used in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction when sinus rate stays high despite a β-blocker. It can cause luminous visual phenomena (phosphenes) because related HCN channels exist in the retina.
  • Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and speeds the sinus rate and AV nodal conduction; it has little effect on block below the AV node.
Use dependence means class IC drugs block more at faster heart rates, which is why their QRS-widening and proarrhythmic effects appear during exercise testing. Class IB drugs are the opposite: they unbind so quickly that they barely affect normal tissue at normal rates.

s23b-s-080301-s1-03.bodyHtml:
Atrioventricular block

AV block is graded by what happens to each P wave.

  • First degree: every P is conducted, but the PR interval is longer than 0.20 s. Usually in the AV node; benign.
  • Second degree, Mobitz type I (Wenckebach): the PR interval lengthens progressively until one P wave is not conducted; the cycle then restarts. The level is almost always the AV node, whose conduction fatigues with each beat. It is common with high vagal tone (athletes, sleep), inferior infarction and AV nodal blocking drugs, and rarely progresses.
  • Second degree, Mobitz type II: the PR interval is constant in conducted beats and P waves are dropped without warning. The block is usually in the His–Purkinje system, often with a wide QRS, and can progress suddenly to complete block.
  • Third degree (complete): no P wave is conducted. Atria and ventricles beat independently (AV dissociation), and the atrial rate is faster than the ventricular escape rate. A junctional escape gives a narrow QRS at about 40–60/min; a ventricular escape gives a wide QRS at about 20–40/min.
In 2:1 block you cannot see whether the PR would have lengthened, so the level is judged from the QRS width and the response to atropine or exercise (better with nodal block, worse with infranodal block).

Re-entry

Re-entry needs two pathways with different conduction speeds and refractory periods, a unidirectional block in one of them and enough slow conduction for the tissue ahead of the wave to recover. Classic examples:

RhythmCircuitCurative ablation target
AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (most common paroxysmal SVT)Fast and slow pathways within or next to the AV nodeSlow pathway
AV re-entrant tachycardiaAV node plus an accessory pathwayAccessory pathway
Typical atrial flutterLarge circuit around the tricuspid annulus in the right atrium (atrial rate about 300/min, often 2:1 conduction → ventricular rate about 150/min)Cavotricuspid isthmus (between the tricuspid annulus and the inferior vena cava)
Monomorphic VT after infarctionSurviving muscle bundles within or around scarScar-related channels

Atrial fibrillation is different: it is driven mostly by rapid firing from muscle sleeves in the pulmonary veins plus many wandering wavelets in remodelled, fibrosed and dilated atria. Pulmonary vein isolation is the core of AF ablation.

Pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern)

An accessory pathway of ordinary myocardium connects atrium and ventricle and conducts without the AV node's delay. Part of the ventricle is therefore activated early through the pathway, giving the triad of a short PR interval, a slurred initial QRS upstroke (delta wave) and a slightly wide QRS, often with secondary ST–T changes. "WPW syndrome" means the pattern plus tachyarrhythmias.

The most common tachycardia is orthodromic AV re-entry (down the AV node, back up the pathway), which is narrow-complex. The dangerous one is atrial fibrillation conducted down the pathway: because the pathway lacks the AV node's rate-limiting refractoriness, ventricular rates can exceed 250/min and degenerate to ventricular fibrillation. Drugs that slow only the AV node push more impulses down the pathway.

Triggered activity and the long QT syndromes

Early afterdepolarizations arise during phase 2–3 when repolarization is prolonged; they trigger torsades de pointes, a polymorphic VT whose QRS axis twists around the baseline. Delayed afterdepolarizations arise after full repolarization when cells are Ca2+-overloaded (digoxin toxicity, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT from ryanodine receptor mutations).

Congenital long QT typeChannel defectTypical trigger
Type 1 (most common)Loss of function of the slow delayed-rectifier K+ current (IKs; KCNQ1)Exercise, especially swimming
Type 2Loss of function of the rapid delayed-rectifier K+ current (IKr; KCNH2/hERG)Sudden noise (alarm clock), emotional stress, the postpartum period
Type 3Gain of function of the cardiac Na+ channel (late Na+ current; SCN5A)Rest and sleep

The autosomal dominant forms were historically called Romano-Ward syndrome. The autosomal recessive form with congenital sensorineural deafness (Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome) involves the IKs channel subunits, which are also needed for endolymph production in the inner ear.

Brugada syndrome, often from loss of function of the same Na+ channel gene, shows a coved ST elevation in V1–V2 and causes polymorphic VT, typically at rest or with fever; it is more often diagnosed in men and in people of East and Southeast Asian ancestry. An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator protects those at high risk.

Do not confuse the two Na+ channel diseases: too much late Na+ current lengthens the QT (long QT type 3); too little Na+ current gives the Brugada pattern.

s23b-s-080401-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Diagnosis

  • Best initial test once HF is suspected: transthoracic echocardiography. It gives the ejection fraction, chamber sizes, wall thickness, valves, diastolic function and pulmonary pressures.
  • Natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP): a normal value makes HF unlikely in a dyspneic patient. Values are lower in obesity and higher with age, renal failure and atrial fibrillation. Sacubitril raises BNP (it blocks its breakdown), so follow NT-proBNP in patients taking an ARNI.
  • Look for the cause: ECG, chest radiograph, blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, thyroid function, iron studies, glucose/HbA1c and lipids; ischemia evaluation in new systolic dysfunction (coronary angiography or noninvasive imaging); cardiac MRI for suspected infiltrative or inflammatory disease.

Classify by EF: HFrEF ≤ 40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥ 50%, and HF with improved EF (previously ≤ 40%, now above 40%: keep the therapy that got it there). Stage it (A at risk, B structural disease without symptoms, C symptomatic, D advanced) and grade symptoms with NYHA class I–IV.

HFrEF: the four drug classes that reduce mortality

ClassExamplesKey cautions
Renin–angiotensin inhibition: ARNI preferred; ACE inhibitor or ARB if ARNI not possibleSacubitril–valsartan; lisinopril, enalapril; losartan, valsartan, candesartanHyperkalemia, rising creatinine, hypotension; angioedema (allow 36 hours off an ACE inhibitor before an ARNI); contraindicated in pregnancy
Evidence-based beta-blockerCarvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprololStart low when euvolemic; do not start during decompensation with low output
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonistSpironolactone, eplerenoneAvoid when potassium is ≥ 5.0 mEq/L or eGFR ≤ 30; gynecomastia with spironolactone (switch to eplerenone)
SGLT2 inhibitorDapagliflozin, empagliflozinGenital mycotic infections, volume depletion, euglycemic ketoacidosis (hold before surgery and during acute illness); benefit is independent of diabetes

Start all four as early as blood pressure, potassium and renal function allow, at low doses, then titrate. Do not wait to reach the maximum dose of one before adding the next.

Added therapies for selected patients

  • Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate: patients who self-identify as Black with NYHA III–IV symptoms despite optimal therapy (mortality benefit), or anyone who cannot take any renin–angiotensin blocker.
  • Ivabradine (blocks the sinoatrial funny current): sinus rhythm, heart rate ≥ 70/min despite a maximally tolerated beta-blocker, EF ≤ 35%.
  • Digoxin: reduces hospitalisation but not mortality; toxicity rises with hypokalemia and renal failure.
  • Loop diuretics: relieve congestion; no proven survival benefit. Use the lowest dose that keeps the patient euvolemic.

Devices

  • Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (primary prevention): EF ≤ 35% with NYHA II–III symptoms despite at least 3 months of guideline therapy, expected survival over 1 year, and more than 40 days after a myocardial infarction.
  • Cardiac resynchronisation therapy: EF ≤ 35%, sinus rhythm, left bundle branch block with QRS ≥ 150 ms, symptoms despite guideline therapy. It can improve EF, symptoms and survival.

Drugs that worsen HFrEF: non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem), thiazolidinediones, NSAIDs, cilostazol, and most class I antiarrhythmics. When a patient with HFrEF and atrial fibrillation is on diltiazem, replace it with a beta-blocker.

HFpEF

  • Diuretics for congestion; treat hypertension, atrial fibrillation, ischemia, obesity and sleep apnea.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF hospitalisation and are a first-line drug class.
  • MRAs and ARNI can be considered, especially at the lower end of the EF range.
  • Long-acting nitrates and routine digoxin do not help.

Lifestyle and nutrition

Daily weights (report a gain of more than about 1 kg in a day or 2 kg in a week), avoiding large sodium loads, fluid restriction only for hyponatremia or refractory congestion, exercise training and cardiac rehabilitation, vaccination against influenza, pneumococcus and COVID-19, and screening for iron deficiency (intravenous iron improves symptoms in HFrEF with iron deficiency). Ask about alcohol and stimulant use.

In a patient with new systolic dysfunction and persistent atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate, restore rate or rhythm control first and repeat the echocardiogram: tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy usually recovers within weeks to months.
