Diuretics for congestion; treat hypertension, atrial fibrillation, ischemia, obesity and sleep apnea.
SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF hospitalisation and are a first-line drug class.
MRAs and ARNI can be considered, especially at the lower end of the EF range.
Long-acting nitrates and routine digoxin do not help.

Daily weights (report a gain of more than about 1 kg in a day or 2 kg in a week), avoiding large sodium loads, fluid restriction only for hyponatremia or refractory congestion, exercise training and cardiac rehabilitation, vaccination against influenza, pneumococcus and COVID-19, and screening for iron deficiency (intravenous iron improves symptoms in HFrEF with iron deficiency). Ask about alcohol and stimulant use.

In a patient with new systolic dysfunction and persistent atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate, restore rate or rhythm control first and repeat the echocardiogram: tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy usually recovers within weeks to months.

s23b-s-080401-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Recognise the haemodynamic profile

Two bedside questions guide therapy: is the patient congested (wet: orthopnea, raised jugular venous pressure, crackles, edema) and is perfusion adequate (warm) or poor (cold: cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure, confusion, oliguria, rising lactate or creatinine)?

ProfileTypical treatment
Warm and wet (most common)IV loop diuretic; add a vasodilator (nitroglycerin) when blood pressure is high
Cold and wetInotrope (dobutamine or milrinone) and diuretic; vasopressor (norepinephrine) if hypotensive; consider mechanical support
Cold and dryCautious fluid if underfilled; reassess for low output
Warm and dryCompensated: optimise oral therapy

Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema

  1. Sit the patient up; give oxygen if hypoxemic.
  2. Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (CPAP or BiPAP) when there is respiratory distress or hypoxemia despite oxygen in a patient who is awake and protecting the airway. It reduces preload and afterload and the work of breathing, and lowers the need for intubation.
  3. IV loop diuretic (furosemide or bumetanide); patients already on an oral loop diuretic need a higher IV dose.
  4. Nitroglycerin for hypertensive presentations (sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema): high doses quickly lower preload and afterload. Avoid with hypotension, recent PDE-5 inhibitor use or right ventricular infarction.
  5. Find and treat the trigger: ischemia or infarction (ECG, troponin), arrhythmia (atrial fibrillation), uncontrolled hypertension, infection, non-adherence to drugs or diet, NSAIDs, thyroid disease, acute valve lesion.

Intubate when the patient is tiring, obtunded, cannot protect the airway or fails noninvasive ventilation. Morphine is no longer used routinely. Continue a chronic beta-blocker unless there is low output or shock; do not start one during decompensation.

Cardiogenic shock

Shock (hypotension with signs of hypoperfusion) caused by pump failure: low cardiac output, high filling pressures (pulmonary capillary wedge pressure above about 15 mm Hg) and high systemic vascular resistance. The commonest cause is a large acute myocardial infarction; others include mechanical complications of infarction (papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal rupture), fulminant myocarditis, end-stage cardiomyopathy and massive pulmonary embolism (right-sided).

  • After an acute MI, emergency revascularisation (usually PCI of the culprit artery) is the treatment that improves survival.
  • Norepinephrine is the usual first vasopressor; add an inotrope (dobutamine or milrinone) for low output. Milrinone (a PDE-3 inhibitor) dilates vessels and is cleared by the kidney.
  • Mechanical circulatory support (intra-aortic balloon pump for mechanical complications, percutaneous ventricular assist devices, venoarterial ECMO) in experienced centres.
  • Echocardiography early, to find a mechanical complication or tamponade.

Acute severe mitral regurgitation

Sudden pulmonary edema, sometimes with a soft or absent murmur, after infarction or in a patient with a floppy mitral valve. Diagnose with echocardiography. Stabilise with afterload reduction (nitroprusside) if blood pressure allows, and an intra-aortic balloon pump; definitive treatment is urgent surgery.

Do not give a vasodilator or a large fluid bolus without checking the profile: nitroprusside in a hypotensive cold patient deepens shock, and fluids in a wet patient worsen edema.

Prognosis

Markers of a worse outlook include hyponatremia, rising creatinine, persistently high natriuretic peptides, inability to tolerate guideline therapy because of hypotension, repeated admissions and NYHA class IV symptoms. Patients with advanced (stage D) HF should be referred for consideration of transplantation, durable left ventricular assist devices or palliative care.

s23b-s-080401-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome: the heart cannot deliver enough blood for the body's needs, or can do so only at raised filling pressures. The symptoms (dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, edema) come from two things: congestion behind the failing chamber and low forward output.

Systolic versus diastolic dysfunction

Systolic dysfunction (HFrEF)Diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF)
Core defectWeak contraction: the end-systolic pressure–volume line is flatterStiff, slow-relaxing ventricle: the end-diastolic pressure–volume curve is steeper
Ejection fraction≤ 40%≥ 50% (41–49% is 'mildly reduced')
VentricleDilated (eccentric remodelling)Normal size, often thick walled (concentric hypertrophy)
Typical causesIschemic heart disease, dilated cardiomyopathy, toxins (alcohol, anthracyclines), myocarditisLong-standing hypertension, older age, obesity, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, infiltrative disease
Extra heart soundS3 (rapid filling into a dilated ventricle)S4 (atrial kick into a stiff ventricle)

On a pressure–volume loop, systolic failure shifts the loop to the right (larger end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes) and narrows it (smaller stroke volume relative to end-diastolic volume). Diastolic failure keeps the volumes near normal but lifts the bottom of the loop: the same filling volume now costs a higher end-diastolic pressure, and that pressure is transmitted back to the lungs.

The Frank–Starling relationship

Stroke volume rises as preload rises, until the curve flattens. A failing ventricle sits on a lower, flatter curve, so extra filling buys little extra output but a lot of extra congestion. Diuretics move the patient leftward along the same curve (less congestion, little loss of output); inotropes move the patient to a higher curve.

Neurohormonal activation: helpful at first, harmful later

  • Sympathetic drive: tachycardia and vasoconstriction maintain pressure, but raise myocardial oxygen demand and cause myocyte loss.
  • Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system: reduced renal perfusion releases renin; angiotensin II constricts arterioles and promotes fibrosis and hypertrophy; aldosterone retains sodium and water and drives myocardial fibrosis.
  • Antidiuretic hormone: water retention, which explains hyponatremia in advanced HF (a poor prognostic sign).
  • Natriuretic peptides: BNP is released by ventricular myocytes in response to wall stretch; ANP mainly by atrial myocytes. Both act through particulate guanylyl cyclase (cGMP) to cause natriuresis and vasodilation. They are degraded by neprilysin.

Every drug that prolongs life in HFrEF blocks one of these maladaptive loops: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and the ARNI (angiotensin II), beta-blockers (sympathetic), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (aldosterone). SGLT2 inhibitors are the exception: their benefit is not explained by glucose lowering, and natriuresis plus metabolic effects on the myocardium are thought to contribute.

Right-sided failure and cor pulmonale

The commonest cause of right heart failure is left heart failure. Cor pulmonale means right ventricular hypertrophy or failure caused by disease of the lungs or pulmonary vessels: COPD, interstitial lung disease, obstructive sleep apnea with hypoventilation, chronic thromboembolism. The key mechanism is hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which raises pulmonary vascular resistance and loads the thin-walled right ventricle. Signs: raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, a loud pulmonic component of S2 and a left parasternal heave.

High-output heart failure

Here cardiac output is high but still inadequate, because systemic vascular resistance is low or metabolic demand is high. Patients have warm extremities, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure. Causes: thyrotoxicosis, severe anemia, large arteriovenous fistula (including dialysis access), Paget disease of bone, pregnancy, sepsis and liver cirrhosis, and wet beriberi (thiamine deficiency: thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase).

Acute mitral regurgitation from chordal or papillary rupture

When a chord tears (myxomatous valve, endocarditis) or a papillary muscle ruptures after infarction, regurgitant blood fills a small, non-compliant left atrium. Left atrial pressure rises abruptly, producing giant v waves on the wedge tracing and flash pulmonary edema. The murmur may be soft or short because atrial and ventricular pressures equalise quickly.

An S3 is normal in children, young adults and pregnancy; after about age 40 it suggests volume overload or systolic dysfunction. An S4 is never normal at any age.

Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (from persistent atrial fibrillation, flutter or incessant supraventricular tachycardia) is one of the few causes of systolic dysfunction that usually reverses once the rate is controlled.

s23b-s-080501-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Is it angina?

Typical angina has three features: substernal pressure-like discomfort, brought on by exertion or emotional stress, and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin within minutes. Two of three is 'atypical'. Estimate the probability of coronary disease from age, sex, symptoms and risk factors before choosing a test.

Choosing the test

SituationReasonable first test
Low probabilityOften no testing; coronary calcium scoring can refine risk
Intermediate probability, no known coronary diseaseCoronary CT angiography or stress testing
Can exercise and resting ECG is interpretableExercise ECG (treadmill), or exercise stress with imaging
Resting ECG uninterpretable for ischemia (ST depression ≥ 1 mm, LVH with repolarisation changes, digoxin, pre-excitation)Stress test with imaging (echocardiography or nuclear perfusion)
Left bundle branch block or ventricular pacingVasodilator (regadenoson or adenosine) perfusion imaging; exercise causes false septal defects
Cannot exercisePharmacologic stress: vasodilator perfusion imaging or dobutamine echocardiography
High-risk stress result or symptoms despite therapyInvasive coronary angiography

Avoid vasodilator agents in active bronchospasm and second- or third-degree AV block; hold caffeine and theophylline beforehand because they block adenosine receptors.

Treatment

Every patient

  • Smoking cessation, a heart-healthy dietary pattern (vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, fish, nuts; limit sodium, processed meat and added sugar), regular physical activity, weight management, cardiac rehabilitation after an event.
  • Aspirin 75–100 mg daily (clopidogrel if aspirin is not tolerated).
  • High-intensity statin; add ezetimibe and then a PCSK9 inhibitor when LDL cholesterol remains 70 mg/dL or higher despite the maximum tolerated statin.
  • Control blood pressure and diabetes; for diabetes with established coronary disease, prefer an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit.
  • Annual influenza vaccination.

Angina relief

  • Sublingual nitroglycerin for attacks, and before activities that bring them on.
  • First-line daily drug: a beta-blocker or a calcium channel blocker. Add the other class, a long-acting nitrate or ranolazine if symptoms continue.

Revascularisation

PCI or bypass surgery relieves angina that persists despite medical therapy. Surgery is favoured for significant left main disease, multivessel disease with diabetes, and multivessel disease with reduced ejection fraction, where it can improve survival. In stable patients without these features, an initial strategy of optimal medical therapy is reasonable.

Vasospastic angina

Young or middle-aged smoker with rest pain at night or early morning and transient ST elevation that resolves with nitroglycerin. Treat with a calcium channel blocker (first line) plus a nitrate, stop smoking and remove triggers (cocaine, amphetamines, triptans). Avoid non-selective beta-blockers, which leave α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed.

Ischemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries

Angina with ischemia on testing but no obstructive lesion, more common in women, is often due to coronary microvascular dysfunction or spasm. Risk factor control and antianginal drugs are used.

A normal exercise ECG in a patient with a baseline LBBB is uninterpretable, not reassuring. Choose the test from the resting ECG first.

s23b-s-080501-ck-02.bodyHtml:
First 10 minutes

  • 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, repeated if pain continues or changes.
  • High-sensitivity troponin at arrival and repeated at 1–3 hours according to the local protocol.
  • Aspirin (chewed) unless truly allergic; oxygen only if saturation is below 90%; sublingual nitroglycerin for pain if blood pressure allows and there is no right ventricular infarction or recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.
  • Consider the other killers of chest pain: aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, esophageal rupture.

STEMI

Criteria: new ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads of at least 1 mm, except in V2–V3, where the threshold is 2 mm in men aged 40 or older, 2.5 mm in men under 40 and 1.5 mm in women. Posterior infarction (ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves; confirm with V7–V9) is treated as a STEMI.

Reperfusion

  • Primary PCI is preferred when it can be done promptly: within 90 minutes of first medical contact at a PCI-capable hospital, or within 120 minutes when the patient must be transferred.
  • Fibrinolysis within 30 minutes of arrival when timely PCI is not possible and symptoms began less than 12 hours earlier, with no contraindication. Then transfer for angiography: urgently if reperfusion fails (less than 50% ST resolution at 60–90 minutes, ongoing pain, instability), otherwise within about 2–24 hours.
  • Absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis include any previous intracranial hemorrhage, a known cerebral vascular lesion or malignant intracranial tumour, ischemic stroke within 3 months, suspected aortic dissection, active bleeding (other than menses) and significant head or facial trauma within 3 months.
  • Cardiogenic shock or acute severe heart failure: emergency angiography and revascularisation regardless of delay.

Right ventricular infarction

Inferior STEMI with hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and clear lungs. Record V4R. The right ventricle depends on preload: give IV fluid, avoid nitrates and diuretics, and reperfuse quickly. Bradycardia or AV block may need atropine or pacing.

NSTE-ACS (unstable angina and NSTEMI)

  • Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, and parenteral anticoagulation (heparin, enoxaparin, or bivalirudin at PCI).
  • Fibrinolysis is not used: it gives no benefit without complete occlusion and adds bleeding.
  • Immediate invasive strategy (within about 2 hours) for refractory angina, hemodynamic instability, acute heart failure, sustained ventricular arrhythmias or mechanical complications.
  • Early invasive (within about 24 hours) for most others with a confirmed NSTEMI or dynamic ST changes; lower-risk patients may have an ischemia-guided approach with stress testing.

After revascularisation

TherapyIndication
Dual antiplatelet therapyAspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel preferred over clopidogrel after ACS) for 12 months by default; shorter in high bleeding risk
High-intensity statinAll; add ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor if LDL cholesterol stays ≥ 70 mg/dL
Beta-blockerClearly indicated with EF ≤ 40%, arrhythmias or ongoing angina; long-term benefit with preserved EF after complete revascularisation is less certain
ACE inhibitor or ARBEF ≤ 40%, hypertension, diabetes or chronic kidney disease
Mineralocorticoid antagonistEF ≤ 40% with heart failure or diabetes, if potassium and renal function allow
Cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation, sexual activity counselling, depression screeningAll

After STEMI with reduced EF, reassess EF at least 40 days after the infarct (90 days after revascularisation) before deciding on a primary-prevention defibrillator; a wearable defibrillator can bridge selected patients.

Do not withhold aspirin because of a history of stomach upset, and do not delay primary PCI to wait for a troponin result when the ECG shows a STEMI.

s23b-s-080501-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Supply, demand and the subendocardium

The myocardium extracts most of the oxygen it receives even at rest, so extra demand must be met by extra coronary flow. Left ventricular flow happens mainly in diastole, when the contracting wall stops squeezing intramural vessels. Tachycardia therefore cuts supply (shorter diastole) while raising demand. The subendocardium is the most vulnerable layer: it is furthest from the epicardial arteries and most compressed during systole.

From plaque to syndrome

  • Stable angina: a fixed narrowing (usually ≥ 70% of the lumen) limits flow only when demand rises. Pain comes with exertion or emotion and settles within minutes of rest or nitroglycerin.
  • Acute coronary syndrome: a plaque ruptures or erodes and a thrombus forms on it. Rupture-prone plaques have a thin fibrous cap, a large lipid-rich necrotic core and many macrophages, whose metalloproteinases digest the cap. Exposed collagen and tissue factor recruit platelets (glycoprotein Ib binding von Willebrand factor, then IIb/IIIa cross-linking by fibrinogen) and start coagulation.
  • A partly occlusive thrombus causes unstable angina (rest or crescendo pain, no troponin rise) or NSTEMI (troponin rise, usually subendocardial). A completely occlusive thrombus causes STEMI, a transmural infarction.
  • Vasospastic (variant) angina: transient spasm of an epicardial artery causes rest pain, often at night or early morning, with transient ST elevation. Triggers include smoking, cocaine and amphetamines, triptans and ergot derivatives, and cold. Coronary angiography may be normal; provocative testing with intracoronary acetylcholine confirms it.

Localising the infarct on the ECG

Leads with ST elevationTerritoryUsual artery
V1–V4Anterior and septal wallLeft anterior descending
I, aVL, V5–V6Lateral wallLeft circumflex or a diagonal branch
II, III, aVFInferior wallRight coronary artery (most); left circumflex in left-dominant hearts
V7–V9 (with ST depression and tall R waves in V1–V3)Posterior wallRight coronary or left circumflex
V4R (right-sided leads)Right ventricleProximal right coronary artery

The tracing above shows ST elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF), more in III than II, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. That pattern favours a right coronary artery occlusion. In a right-dominant circulation the right coronary artery also supplies the sinoatrial node (in most people) and the atrioventricular node, so inferior infarcts are often accompanied by sinus bradycardia or AV block, and by right ventricular infarction when the occlusion is proximal.

Biomarkers

Cardiac troponin (I or T) is the marker of choice: it rises within a few hours of injury (earlier with high-sensitivity assays), peaks at about 24 hours and stays raised for 7–10 days. CK-MB rises and falls faster, returning to normal within 2–3 days, which made it useful for spotting reinfarction; a fresh rise in troponin above a falling baseline serves the same purpose today.

What the tissue shows

  • Myocytes stop contracting within about a minute of ischemia; irreversible injury starts after roughly 20–40 minutes, beginning in the subendocardium and spreading outward as a 'wavefront'.
  • The infarct undergoes coagulation necrosis: the outline of dead cells persists while nuclei disappear.
  • When flow is restored after cells are already lethally injured, calcium floods in and causes contraction band necrosis; reperfusion also brings free radicals (reperfusion injury) and hemorrhage into the infarct.
  • Gross appearance: no visible change for many hours (triphenyltetrazolium chloride stain shows unstained pale infarct early), then pallor, a yellow soft centre with a hyperemic border around days 3–10, and finally a white scar.

The infarct is weakest while macrophages remove dead muscle and before collagen is laid down, roughly days 3–14. Free wall rupture, septal rupture and papillary muscle rupture cluster in this window.

Women, older adults and people with diabetes more often present with dyspnea, fatigue, nausea or epigastric discomfort rather than classic chest pressure. Obtain an ECG within 10 minutes for any of these presentations.

Drugs that lower oxygen demand or raise supply

DrugMechanismMain anti-ischemic effectNotable adverse effects
Nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide)Release nitric oxide → soluble guanylyl cyclase → cGMP → myosin light chain dephosphorylationVenodilation lowers preload and wall stress; also dilate epicardial arteries and relieve spasmHeadache, flushing, orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia; tolerance without a nitrate-free interval; dangerous hypotension with PDE-5 inhibitors
Beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol)β1 blockadeLower heart rate and contractility; longer diastole improves perfusionBradycardia, AV block, fatigue, bronchospasm with non-selective agents; avoid in vasospastic and cocaine-related angina
Calcium channel blockersBlock L-type channels; dihydropyridines act mainly on arteriolar smooth muscle, verapamil and diltiazem also on the heartLower afterload; verapamil and diltiazem also lower rate; all prevent coronary spasmEdema and flushing (dihydropyridines); constipation, bradycardia, AV block (verapamil)
RanolazineInhibits the late inward sodium current, reducing calcium overloadLess diastolic wall tension without changing heart rate or blood pressureQT prolongation, constipation, dizziness; many CYP3A4 interactions

Nitrates and beta-blockers complement each other: nitrates cause reflex tachycardia and beta-blockers prevent it; beta-blockers enlarge the ventricle slightly by slowing the rate, and nitrates shrink it by lowering preload.

Antiplatelet drugs

  • Aspirin: irreversibly acetylates COX-1, so platelets (which have no nucleus to make new enzyme) cannot make thromboxane A2 for their 7–10 day life.
  • P2Y12 (ADP receptor) blockers: clopidogrel and prasugrel are prodrugs that bind irreversibly; clopidogrel needs activation by CYP2C19, so poor metabolisers get less effect. Prasugrel is more potent and is avoided after stroke or transient ischemic attack. Ticagrelor binds reversibly, needs no activation and can cause dyspnea; it is not combined with aspirin doses above 100 mg/day.
  • Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (eptifibatide, tirofiban): block the final common pathway of aggregation; used in selected patients during PCI.

Anticoagulants used in acute coronary syndrome

Unfractionated heparin (binds antithrombin; monitored by aPTT; reversed by protamine), enoxaparin (mainly anti-factor Xa; renally cleared), bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitor) and fondaparinux (factor Xa via antithrombin; not used alone during PCI because of catheter thrombosis).

Fibrinolytics

Alteplase, reteplase and tenecteplase convert plasminogen to plasmin, which digests fibrin in the clot. They help only when there is complete occlusion with ST elevation and benefit falls steeply with time. The main hazard is bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage.

Coronary steal

Vasodilator stress agents (adenosine and the selective A2A agonist regadenoson, or dipyridamole, which raises adenosine) dilate healthy coronary arterioles. Arterioles beyond a severe stenosis are already maximally dilated, so flow is diverted toward normal territory and the stenotic region shows relatively reduced perfusion on imaging.

Lipid lowering for secondary prevention

Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, raise hepatic LDL receptors and stabilise plaques. Ezetimibe blocks intestinal cholesterol uptake (NPC1L1); PCSK9 inhibitors prevent LDL receptor degradation.

Do not give a nitrate within 24 hours of sildenafil or vardenafil, or within 48 hours of tadalafil: both pathways raise cGMP and the combination can cause profound hypotension.

s23b-s-080601-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Approach to a new cardiomyopathy

  • Best initial test: transthoracic echocardiography (chamber size, wall thickness, ejection fraction, outflow gradient, valves). Add ECG, chest radiograph, BNP or NT-proBNP.
  • Exclude ischemia in any new reduced ejection fraction with risk factors (coronary angiography or CT coronary angiography).
  • Look for reversible causes: alcohol and stimulant history, thyroid function, iron studies, HIV where appropriate, tachyarrhythmia, thiamine status in malnutrition or heavy alcohol use, recent pregnancy, chemotherapy exposure.
  • Cardiac MRI characterises tissue (myocarditis, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, infiltration, scar). Endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for suspected giant cell myocarditis, unexplained fulminant failure or uncertain infiltration.

Dilated cardiomyopathy

Treat as heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: guideline-directed therapy (an ARNI, ACE inhibitor or ARB; an evidence-based β-blocker; a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; an SGLT2 inhibitor), loop diuretics for congestion, and device therapy (ICD, cardiac resynchronization) when criteria are met after optimised medical therapy. Treat the cause:

  • Alcohol: complete abstinence can produce substantial recovery of ejection fraction.
  • Tachycardia-induced: rate or rhythm control.
  • Peripartum: standard therapy adjusted for pregnancy (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNIs and mineralocorticoid antagonists are avoided during pregnancy); anticoagulation is considered when the ejection fraction is very low. Counsel that a later pregnancy carries a high risk of relapse and death, especially if function has not returned to normal.
  • Takotsubo: supportive care and standard heart failure therapy until recovery; avoid inotropes that increase catecholamine load when outflow obstruction is present.
  • Familial DCM: screen first-degree relatives with ECG and echocardiography, and offer genetic testing.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Diagnosis: echocardiography or cardiac MRI showing unexplained left ventricular wall thickness of 15 mm or more (lower thresholds in relatives). Measure the outflow gradient at rest and with provocation (Valsalva, standing, exercise).

  • Symptomatic obstruction, first line: a non-vasodilating β-blocker titrated to effect; if not tolerated or ineffective, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil or diltiazem) in patients without severe obstruction or low blood pressure. Next options: disopyramide, or a cardiac myosin inhibitor (mavacamten) with regular echocardiographic monitoring of ejection fraction.
  • Refractory obstruction: septal reduction (surgical myectomy or alcohol septal ablation) at experienced centres.
  • Avoid: arterial vasodilators (dihydropyridines, nitrates, high-dose ACE inhibitors), aggressive diuresis and dehydration, digoxin, all of which shrink the ventricle or increase contractility and worsen obstruction. Treat hypotension in obstructive HCM with intravenous fluids and phenylephrine, not inotropes.
  • Sudden death prevention: an ICD for prior cardiac arrest or sustained ventricular tachycardia, and as primary prevention when risk markers are present (sudden death in a close relative, unexplained syncope, massive wall thickness of 30 mm or more, apical aneurysm, low ejection fraction, extensive late gadolinium enhancement). Antiarrhythmic drugs do not replace an ICD.
  • Atrial fibrillation in HCM: anticoagulate regardless of the CHA2DS2-VASc score.
  • Family: genetic counselling, cascade genetic testing for a known familial variant, and periodic ECG and echocardiography in first-degree relatives.
  • Exercise: shared decision-making; most patients can do moderate exercise, and participation in competitive sport is individualised after expert evaluation.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy and cardiac amyloidosis

  • Suspect cardiac amyloidosis in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction plus thick walls and low QRS voltage, intolerance of antihypertensives, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis or atrial fibrillation in an older adult.
  • First exclude AL amyloidosis: serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation. If no monoclonal protein is present, a positive technetium-labelled bone-tracer scan (for example pyrophosphate) establishes ATTR cardiomyopathy without biopsy; send TTR genetic testing.
  • ATTR therapy: a transthyretin stabiliser (tafamidis) slows progression; diuretics for congestion. AL amyloidosis needs urgent hematology care (plasma-cell–directed chemotherapy).
  • Rate-control drugs are poorly tolerated: β-blockers and calcium channel blockers can precipitate hypotension and low output, and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers bind amyloid fibrils.
In obstructive HCM, the drugs that help most patients with heart failure (vasodilators, diuretics, digoxin) can make the patient worse. When a young patient's murmur and symptoms worsen after a nitrate or a diuretic, think outflow obstruction.

s23b-s-080601-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Mechanical complications after myocardial infarction

Mechanical complications are now uncommon in the era of prompt primary PCI but carry high mortality. Late presenters with a large first infarct are at greatest risk.

  • Any sudden hemodynamic deterioration or new murmur after infarction: perform urgent bedside echocardiography first.
  • Papillary muscle rupture (acute severe mitral regurgitation): afterload reduction (for example nitroprusside if pressure allows), diuretics, and temporary mechanical circulatory support (intra-aortic balloon pump or other devices) as a bridge to emergency surgical mitral valve repair or replacement. Medical therapy alone has very high mortality.
  • Ventricular septal rupture: confirm with echocardiography (colour flow across the septum); a right heart catheter shows an oxygen saturation step-up in the right ventricle. Stabilise with afterload reduction and mechanical support, and arrange surgical (or, in selected patients, transcatheter) closure.
  • Free wall rupture: tamponade with pulseless electrical activity or profound shock; pericardiocentesis only as a temporizing bridge to emergency surgical repair.
  • Left ventricular thrombus (most often after a large anterior infarct with an akinetic or aneurysmal apex): add oral anticoagulation for at least about 3 months, then reassess with imaging.
  • True aneurysm: guideline-directed heart failure therapy; consider surgery for refractory heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias. Pseudoaneurysm: surgical repair because of rupture risk.

Right ventricular infarction

Suspect it in every inferior STEMI: record right-sided leads (ST elevation in V4R). Treat with urgent reperfusion. Support preload with intravenous fluid boluses when hypotensive and the lungs are clear; avoid nitrates, morphine-induced venodilation and diuretics. Inotropes (for example dobutamine) are added if fluids alone fail. High-grade AV block is common and may need temporary pacing.

Myocarditis

  • Hospitalise patients with heart failure, arrhythmias or raised troponin; monitor for ventricular arrhythmias and heart block.
  • Treat heart failure and arrhythmias in the usual way; use temporary mechanical support for fulminant presentations at centres that can provide it.
  • Immunosuppression is reserved for specific forms (giant cell myocarditis, cardiac sarcoidosis, eosinophilic myocarditis, immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis, which needs high-dose glucocorticoids and stopping the drug).
  • Avoid NSAIDs when myocarditis is the dominant process in heart failure. Advise no competitive sports or strenuous exercise for about 3–6 months, then re-evaluate (ECG, echocardiography, ambulatory rhythm monitoring and often exercise testing) before return.

Prognosis

  • Most mild viral myocarditis resolves; a minority progress to DCM.
  • Takotsubo usually recovers fully within weeks, but in-hospital complications (shock, arrhythmia, LV thrombus) are similar to those of acute coronary syndrome.
  • Peripartum cardiomyopathy recovers in roughly half of patients; non-recovery predicts relapse in a later pregnancy.

s23b-s-080601-s1-01.bodyHtml:
A cardiomyopathy is a disease of the heart muscle itself that is not explained by coronary disease, hypertension, valve disease or congenital shunts alone. Exam questions sort them by what the ventricle looks like and which phase of the cycle fails: a big, weak ventricle (dilated), a thick, stiff ventricle (hypertrophic) or a normal-sized but stiff ventricle (restrictive).

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)

The most common cardiomyopathy. All four chambers enlarge, the walls are thin relative to the cavity, and contraction is globally weak, so the defect is systolic (reduced ejection fraction). Myocytes add sarcomeres in series, giving eccentric hypertrophy: heart weight rises even though the walls look thin.

Cause groupExamples and clues
Genetic (familial)Often autosomal dominant; truncating variants in TTN (titin) are the most common single cause; lamin A/C variants add conduction disease and sudden death; dystrophin defects (Duchenne, Becker)
ToxicLong-term heavy alcohol use; anthracyclines (cumulative, dose-dependent); cocaine; methamphetamine
Infectious / post-inflammatoryViral myocarditis (enteroviruses such as coxsackie B, adenovirus, parvovirus B19); Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), with apical aneurysm and right bundle branch block
Nutritional / metabolicThiamine deficiency (wet beriberi), selenium deficiency, hypothyroidism, hemochromatosis (early)
Pregnancy-relatedPeripartum cardiomyopathy: last month of pregnancy to about 5 months postpartum
Rate-relatedTachycardia-induced (persistent fast atrial fibrillation); reverses with rate or rhythm control
Stress-inducedTakotsubo: transient, catecholamine-driven

Findings: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, edema; displaced, diffuse apical impulse; S3; functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation as the annulus stretches. Chest radiograph shows a globular cardiac silhouette; echocardiography shows dilated chambers with a low ejection fraction.

Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy

Typically a postmenopausal woman after a sudden emotional or physical stressor. Presents exactly like an acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, ST elevation or T inversion, troponin rise), but coronary angiography shows no culprit obstruction. The left ventricular apex balloons while the base contracts vigorously. The mechanism is a catecholamine surge that stuns the apical myocardium. Function usually recovers within weeks.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)

The most common inherited heart disease, usually autosomal dominant with variable penetrance. Variants are in sarcomere genes, most often MYH7 (β-myosin heavy chain) and MYBPC3 (cardiac myosin-binding protein C). Histology shows myocyte disarray with interstitial fibrosis.

  • Hypertrophy is often asymmetric, thickest in the interventricular septum. The thick, stiff ventricle relaxes poorly, so the defect is mainly diastolic; an S4 is common and the ejection fraction is normal or high.
  • In the obstructive form, the septum narrows the left ventricular outflow tract and the anterior mitral leaflet is drawn toward it in systole (systolic anterior motion), producing a dynamic obstruction and often mitral regurgitation.
  • Obstruction worsens when the ventricle is smaller (less preload) or the aorta is easier to empty into (less afterload), and when contractility rises.
  • Sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmia, often during exertion, is the feared outcome and the classic cause of sudden death in young athletes.
ManoeuvreEffect on LV sizeHCM murmurAortic stenosis murmur
Valsalva strain, standing upSmaller (less venous return)LouderSofter
Squatting, passive leg raiseLarger (more venous return)SofterLouder
Sustained handgripLarger (higher afterload)SofterSofter
Vasodilator (e.g. nitrate)Smaller (lower preload and afterload)LouderLouder
HCM is the murmur that gets louder when the ventricle gets smaller. A systolic murmur that grows with Valsalva or on standing points to HCM (or mitral valve prolapse, whose click moves earlier); almost every other murmur softens.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy

Walls are stiff but not necessarily thick, cavities are normal or small, and both atria enlarge because they fill against high ventricular pressures. Systolic function is preserved until late. Right-sided congestion (raised jugular venous pressure, Kussmaul sign, hepatomegaly, edema) often dominates.

  • Amyloidosis: immunoglobulin light chain (AL) or transthyretin (ATTR; wild-type in older men, hereditary variants such as V122I that are more common in people of West African ancestry). Thick walls on echocardiography with low QRS voltage on the ECG is the classic mismatch. Congo red staining shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome often precedes ATTR cardiac disease by years.
  • Sarcoidosis: noncaseating granulomas; heart block and ventricular arrhythmias.
  • Hemochromatosis: iron deposition (can also give a dilated phenotype).
  • Endomyocardial fibrosis and Löffler endocarditis (eosinophilic, with hypereosinophilia).
  • Post-radiation fibrosis.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis look alike at the bedside. A thickened or calcified pericardium, marked respiratory variation in ventricular filling and a normal or only mildly raised BNP favour constriction; thick myocardium, very high BNP and abnormal myocardial tissue on MRI favour restriction.

Hypertensive heart disease and ventricular hypertrophy

Chronic pressure overload makes myocytes add sarcomeres in parallel: concentric hypertrophy with a thick wall and normal or small cavity. Early consequences are impaired relaxation (S4, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction), atrial enlargement and atrial fibrillation; late consequences include systolic failure. The ECG shows tall left-sided voltages with a repolarization ("strain") pattern. Right ventricular hypertrophy follows pressure overload of the right ventricle (pulmonary hypertension, pulmonic stenosis, congenital shunts) and gives right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1.

Pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis) → sarcomeres in parallel → concentric hypertrophy. Volume overload (regurgitant valves, DCM) → sarcomeres in series → eccentric hypertrophy.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy

Fibrofatty replacement of mainly right ventricular myocardium, usually from desmosome gene variants (for example plakophilin-2). It causes ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death in young people and is a reason athletes are screened when symptoms or a family history suggest it.

s23b-s-080601-s1-02.bodyHtml:
Myocarditis

Inflammation of the myocardium with myocyte injury. Causes:

  • Viral (most common in high-income countries): enteroviruses such as coxsackie B, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6, SARS-CoV-2.
  • Other infections: Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas), Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme carditis, mainly AV block), diphtheria toxin, Toxoplasma in immunosuppression.
  • Immune and drug-related: immune checkpoint inhibitors (can be fulminant), mRNA COVID-19 vaccines (rare; mostly young males within days of a dose), hypersensitivity (eosinophilic) myocarditis from drugs, systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, giant cell myocarditis.

The typical patient is a young adult with chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations or new heart failure days to weeks after a viral illness. Troponin is raised with unobstructed coronaries. Cardiac MRI shows edema and late gadolinium enhancement in a non-coronary pattern (subepicardial or mid-wall rather than subendocardial). The reference standard is endomyocardial biopsy: a lymphocytic infiltrate with adjacent myocyte necrosis. Giant cell myocarditis shows multinucleated giant cells with eosinophils and has a poor prognosis without immunosuppression.

Mechanical and other complications of myocardial infarction

The timing of complications follows the healing of the infarct. The necrotic wall is softest about 3–14 days after infarction, when macrophages have removed dead myocytes but collagen has not yet been laid down. This is the window for ruptures.

s23b-s-080701-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Diagnosis of acute pericarditis

Diagnose acute pericarditis with at least two of: pleuritic, positional chest pain; a friction rub; new widespread ST elevation or PR depression; a new or worsening pericardial effusion. Supporting findings are raised C-reactive protein and evidence of pericardial inflammation on imaging.

  • Initial tests: ECG, chest radiograph, transthoracic echocardiography (all patients), C-reactive protein, troponin, complete blood count, renal function. Targeted tests (TB testing, ANA, TSH, blood cultures, HIV) depend on the clinical picture.
  • A raised troponin means myopericarditis (myocardial involvement): admit for monitoring, avoid high-dose NSAIDs if left ventricular function is reduced, and restrict exercise for longer.

Who needs admission?

Most patients with uncomplicated idiopathic or viral pericarditis are managed as outpatients. Admit and investigate when any high-risk feature is present: fever above 38 °C, subacute onset over days to weeks, a large effusion (more than 20 mm in diastole) or tamponade, failure to improve after a week of NSAIDs, immunosuppression, trauma, oral anticoagulant therapy, or myopericarditis.

Treatment of acute pericarditis

  • First line: a high-dose NSAID (ibuprofen) or aspirin, tapered once symptoms and CRP settle, plus colchicine for about 3 months (about 6 months for recurrent disease), which halves the risk of recurrence. Add gastric protection.
  • After myocardial infarction: use aspirin; other NSAIDs and glucocorticoids are avoided because they may impair healing of the infarct and increase rupture risk.
  • Glucocorticoids are second line (contraindication or failure of NSAIDs and colchicine, or specific indications such as autoimmune disease or pregnancy beyond 20 weeks, when NSAIDs are avoided). Used early in viral pericarditis, they increase recurrences.
  • Recurrent pericarditis that depends on steroids or fails colchicine: interleukin-1 blockade (for example rilonacept or anakinra) at specialist centres.
  • Restrict strenuous exercise until symptoms and CRP resolve (at least 3 months for athletes; longer for myopericarditis).
  • Specific causes: uremic pericarditis → start or intensify dialysis; tuberculous pericarditis → antituberculous therapy; purulent pericarditis → drainage plus intravenous antibiotics; hypothyroid effusion → levothyroxine.

Pericardial effusion and tamponade

  • Echocardiography is the test of choice: effusion size, right atrial systolic collapse, right ventricular diastolic collapse, a plethoric inferior vena cava, and exaggerated respiratory variation of mitral and tricuspid inflow.
  • Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis supported by echocardiography. Treat with urgent pericardiocentesis (echocardiography-guided) or surgical drainage. Give intravenous fluid as a bridge in hypovolemic patients.
  • Avoid: diuretics and venodilators (they lower the filling pressure the heart depends on) and, when possible, intubation with positive-pressure ventilation before drainage (raised intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and can precipitate arrest).
  • Send fluid for cell count, protein and LDH, glucose, Gram stain and culture, acid-fast stain and culture or adenosine deaminase, and cytology.
  • Malignant or recurrent effusions: extended catheter drainage, a pericardial window (surgical or balloon) and treatment of the cancer.
  • Hemopericardium from type A aortic dissection or ventricular rupture: emergency surgery; pericardiocentesis only as a temporizing measure if the patient is arresting.

Constrictive pericarditis

  • Confirm with echocardiography (septal bounce, respiratory variation, preserved tissue Doppler velocities), CT or MRI (thickened, calcified pericardium) and, when needed, simultaneous left and right heart catheterisation (discordant respiratory changes in ventricular systolic pressures).
  • Transient (inflammatory) constriction after recent pericarditis may resolve with anti-inflammatory therapy.
  • Chronic constriction: diuretics relieve congestion temporarily; the definitive treatment is surgical pericardiectomy, best done before severe functional decline. Results are worse after radiation-induced constriction.
A raised troponin turns pericarditis into myopericarditis; a fever above 38 °C, a large effusion or NSAID failure turns outpatient care into admission. These high-risk features are frequent "next step" pivots.

s23b-s-080701-s1-01.bodyHtml:
The pericardium is a two-layered sac: a fibrous outer layer and a serous layer whose visceral part (the epicardium) covers the heart. Normally 15–50 mL of fluid lubricates the space. The fibrous layer stretches little, which explains both tamponade (fluid that accumulates quickly) and constriction (a scarred, rigid sac).

Acute pericarditis

Causes: most cases in high-income countries are idiopathic or viral (enteroviruses such as coxsackie B, echovirus). Others: tuberculosis (the leading cause where TB is common), bacterial infection (purulent), autoimmune disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis), drugs causing drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid), uremia, malignancy (lung and breast cancer, lymphoma), radiation, and injury to the pericardium (early after transmural infarction, weeks after infarction or cardiac surgery).

Pathology: most forms are fibrinous (a rough, shaggy fibrin coat; classic in uremia, after infarction and in rheumatic fever) or serous (viral, autoimmune). Purulent pericarditis follows bacterial spread; caseous pericarditis is tuberculous; hemorrhagic pericarditis suggests malignancy or tuberculosis.

Presentation: sharp, pleuritic chest pain that improves when sitting up and leaning forward and worsens lying flat. Pain may radiate to the trapezius ridge because the diaphragmatic pericardium is innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5). A scratchy friction rub, best heard at the left sternal border with the patient leaning forward, may have up to three components.

ECG: inflammation of the epicardium injures the subepicardial myocardium, producing diffuse concave ST elevation in most limb and precordial leads, with PR depression (atrial injury). Lead aVR shows the mirror image: PR elevation and ST depression. Unlike infarction there are no Q waves and no territorial reciprocal ST depression, and T waves invert only after the ST segments have returned to baseline. Uremic pericarditis often lacks these ECG changes because the myocardium is not inflamed.

FeatureAcute pericarditisST-elevation MI
ST shape and distributionConcave, diffuse, not territorialOften convex, in a coronary territory
Reciprocal ST depressionOnly in aVR (and sometimes V1)In the opposite leads
PR segmentDepressed (elevated in aVR)Usually normal
Q wavesAbsentDevelop
PainPleuritic, positionalPressure-like, not positional

Pericardial effusion and tamponade

How fast fluid accumulates matters more than how much. A slowly growing effusion stretches the sac and can reach 1–2 L with little effect, while 100–200 mL that appears in minutes (trauma, free wall rupture, aortic dissection into the pericardium) can cause tamponade.

Tamponade is compression of the heart by pericardial pressure, which limits diastolic filling. The intrapericardial pressure is transmitted to all four chambers, so diastolic pressures equalise (right atrial, right ventricular diastolic, pulmonary artery diastolic and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures become similar). Because filling throughout diastole is restricted, the jugular venous y descent is blunted or absent, while the x descent is preserved.

  • Beck triad: hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds.
  • Pulsus paradoxus: an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mm Hg. Inspiration increases venous return to the right ventricle; in a fixed pericardial volume, the septum bows into the left ventricle (ventricular interdependence), reducing left ventricular filling and stroke volume. Pulsus paradoxus also occurs in severe asthma and COPD exacerbations.
  • Tachycardia, low QRS voltage and electrical alternans (beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude as the heart swings within a large effusion).
  • Chest radiograph: an enlarged, rounded ("water-bottle") silhouette with a large chronic effusion; the size can be normal in acute tamponade.

Constrictive pericarditis

A thick, fibrotic and sometimes calcified pericardium encases the heart. Early diastolic filling is rapid until the ventricles hit the rigid shell, then stops abruptly.

  • Causes: tuberculosis (worldwide), prior cardiac surgery, mediastinal radiation (for example for Hodgkin lymphoma), viral or idiopathic pericarditis, connective tissue disease.
  • Findings: chronic right-sided congestion out of proportion to other signs (raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, ascites, edema), Kussmaul sign (jugular venous pressure rises or fails to fall on inspiration), a pericardial knock (an early diastolic sound earlier and higher-pitched than an S3, caused by the abrupt halt of ventricular filling), a prominent, steep y descent, and a "dip-and-plateau" (square-root) ventricular diastolic pressure tracing.
  • Patients can be misdiagnosed with liver disease because of ascites and hepatomegaly.
TamponadeConstrictive pericarditis
OnsetAcute or subacuteChronic
Pulsus paradoxusTypicalUncommon or mild
Kussmaul signUncommonTypical
Jugular y descentBlunted or absentProminent and steep
Extra soundNone; heart sounds muffledPericardial knock
ImagingEffusion with chamber collapseThick or calcified pericardium
Kussmaul sign belongs to constriction and restrictive cardiomyopathy; pulsus paradoxus belongs to tamponade. Both have a raised jugular venous pressure, so the y descent and the respiratory signs separate them.

Pericarditis after myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery

  • Early (peri-infarction) pericarditis, 1–3 days after a transmural infarct: local fibrinous inflammation over the necrotic wall.
  • Post-cardiac injury syndrome (post-infarction or Dressler syndrome, post-pericardiotomy syndrome): weeks after the injury, with fever, pleuritic pain, pericardial and pleural effusions and raised inflammatory markers. Mechanism: an autoimmune response to myocardial and pericardial antigens released by the injury.
Drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline, anti-TNF agents) commonly causes serositis, including pericarditis; it is associated with anti-histone antibodies and resolves after the drug is stopped.

s23b-s-080801-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Evaluating a murmur

  • Transthoracic echocardiography is the test of choice for any diastolic or continuous murmur, any murmur grade 3 or louder, any murmur with symptoms or other abnormal findings (abnormal S2, ejection click, radiation, abnormal ECG).
  • A soft (grade 1–2), short, mid-systolic murmur at the left sternal border with a normal S2, no symptoms and no other findings is usually innocent (functional): common in children (vibratory, louder lying down and softer on standing), in pregnancy and with high output states (fever, anemia, thyrotoxicosis). Reassurance is appropriate.
  • Severity on echocardiography for aortic stenosis: severe when peak velocity is 4 m/s or more, mean gradient 40 mm Hg or more, or valve area 1.0 cm2 or less.

Aortic stenosis

  • Valve replacement is indicated for severe stenosis with symptoms, and for asymptomatic severe stenosis when the left ventricular ejection fraction falls below 50% or when the patient needs other cardiac surgery. Exercise testing can unmask symptoms in apparently asymptomatic patients.
  • Transcatheter (TAVR) versus surgical (SAVR) replacement is chosen by a heart team using age and life expectancy, surgical risk, valve and vascular anatomy, and patient preference. In general, TAVR is favoured in older patients (for example older than about 80) or in those with high surgical risk, SAVR in younger, lower-risk patients (for example younger than about 65) or with anatomy unsuitable for TAVR, and either may be chosen in between.
  • No medical therapy slows stenosis. Treat hypertension cautiously. Balloon valvuloplasty is only a temporary bridge.

Aortic regurgitation

  • Chronic severe regurgitation: surgery for symptoms, or for an asymptomatic patient with an ejection fraction of 55% or less or a markedly dilated left ventricle. Treat hypertension (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) in those who are not candidates.
  • Acute severe regurgitation (endocarditis, type A dissection): urgent surgery. An intra-aortic balloon pump is contraindicated (inflation in diastole worsens regurgitation). β-Blockers are used cautiously because the tachycardia shortens diastole and limits the regurgitant volume.

Mitral regurgitation

  • Severe primary regurgitation: surgery (repair preferred over replacement) for symptoms, or when asymptomatic with left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction 60% or less, or end-systolic diameter 40 mm or more). Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair is an option for patients at high surgical risk.
  • Severe secondary regurgitation: optimise guideline-directed heart failure therapy and cardiac resynchronization first; transcatheter edge-to-edge repair helps selected patients who remain symptomatic.
  • Acute severe regurgitation: afterload reduction and mechanical support as a bridge to urgent surgery.

Mitral stenosis

  • Symptoms: β-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers slow the heart and lengthen diastolic filling; diuretics relieve congestion.
  • Anticoagulation: rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation, prior embolism or left atrial thrombus requires a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin); DOACs are not used in moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis.
  • Severe symptomatic stenosis with favourable anatomy: percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy; otherwise surgery.
  • Pregnancy: the rise in blood volume and heart rate can precipitate pulmonary edema. Use a β1-selective blocker (for example metoprolol) and cautious diuretics; balloon commissurotomy during pregnancy for refractory symptoms.
  • Secondary prevention of rheumatic fever: long-term intramuscular benzathine penicillin G every 3–4 weeks.

Prosthetic valves

  • Mechanical valve: lifelong warfarin (higher INR targets for mitral position or added risk factors). DOACs are contraindicated: they caused more valve thrombosis and bleeding than warfarin in a trial of mechanical valves.
  • Bioprosthetic valve: aspirin long term; a vitamin K antagonist for the first 3–6 months may be reasonable when bleeding risk is low. DOACs may be used for atrial fibrillation in patients with a bioprosthetic valve.
  • New dyspnea, a muffled mechanical click or an embolic event in a patient with a mechanical valve: urgent echocardiography (TTE and TEE) or fluoroscopy for thrombosis.
  • Infective endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue or perforate the oral mucosa: prosthetic valves (including transcatheter valves), prosthetic material used for valve repair (annuloplasty rings, chords), prior endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, and valvulopathy after heart transplant. A single dose of amoxicillin 30–60 minutes before the procedure is standard.
Two warfarin-only situations: a mechanical heart valve, and atrial fibrillation with moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. A question offering a DOAC in either setting is offering the wrong answer.

Valve lesions are either stenosis (the open valve obstructs forward flow, a pressure load on the chamber behind it) or regurgitation (the closed valve leaks, a volume load). The timing of the murmur follows directly from when each valve should be open or closed.

Murmur map

LesionTiming and shapeWhere heard, radiationAssociated signs
Aortic stenosisSystolic, crescendo–decrescendo (ejection), peaks later as severity increasesRight upper sternal border → carotidsSlow-rising, weak carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus); soft or single S2; paradoxical S2 splitting; S4; ejection click if the valve is bicuspid and mobile
Mitral regurgitationHolosystolic, blowing, plateauApex → left axillaS3 with severe volume load; displaced apex
Mitral valve prolapseMid-systolic click, then late systolic murmurApexClick and murmur move earlier with a smaller ventricle (standing, Valsalva)
Tricuspid regurgitationHolosystolicLeft lower sternal borderLouder with inspiration; large v waves in the jugular pulse; pulsatile liver
Aortic regurgitationEarly diastolic, high-pitched, decrescendoLeft sternal border (right sternal border if the root is dilated); best sitting forward in expirationWide pulse pressure, bounding pulses, head bobbing; Austin Flint mid-diastolic rumble
Mitral stenosisOpening snap, then low-pitched diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation (lost in atrial fibrillation)Apex, with the bell, patient in left lateral positionLoud S1; signs of left atrial enlargement and pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonic stenosisSystolic ejectionLeft upper sternal borderLouder with inspiration; wide S2 split

Manoeuvres

  • Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart: right-sided murmurs get louder (Carvallo sign in tricuspid regurgitation).
  • More venous return (squatting, passive leg raise) makes most murmurs louder; less venous return (standing, Valsalva strain) makes most softer. The exceptions are hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (louder with less preload) and mitral valve prolapse (click earlier and murmur longer with less preload).
  • Higher afterload (sustained handgrip) increases backward flow: louder mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation and ventricular septal defect murmurs; softer aortic stenosis and HCM murmurs.
  • Lower afterload (amyl nitrite, other vasodilators) has the opposite effect.

Aortic stenosis

  • Age-related calcific degeneration of a trileaflet valve is the most common cause in older adults. It resembles atherosclerosis (lipid deposition, inflammation, then dystrophic calcification) and shares its risk factors, with normal serum calcium.
  • A bicuspid aortic valve (about 1–2% of people; more common in men, and associated with Turner syndrome and coarctation of the aorta) calcifies decades earlier and is often accompanied by ascending aortic dilation.
  • Rheumatic aortic stenosis almost always coexists with mitral valve disease.
  • The ventricle responds to pressure overload with concentric hypertrophy. Symptoms (exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope) mark a sharp fall in survival without valve replacement. Angina results from increased demand of thick muscle and reduced coronary perfusion; syncope from fixed output that cannot rise during exertion.
  • Heyde syndrome: gastrointestinal bleeding from angiodysplasia in severe aortic stenosis. High shear across the valve unfolds von Willebrand factor, which is then cleaved by ADAMTS13, leaving too few high-molecular-weight multimers.

Aortic regurgitation

Causes are either leaflet disease (bicuspid valve, endocarditis, rheumatic disease) or aortic root dilation (long-standing hypertension, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, ankylosing spondylitis, syphilitic aortitis, aortic dissection). Chronic regurgitation causes combined volume and pressure overload with eccentric hypertrophy and a very large stroke volume; the regurgitant runoff lowers diastolic pressure, widening the pulse pressure. Acute severe regurgitation (endocarditis, dissection) gives no time for dilation: pulmonary edema and shock with a soft, short murmur and no wide pulse pressure.

Mitral regurgitation and prolapse

  • Primary (degenerative) regurgitation is a disease of the valve itself: myxomatous degeneration (prolapse; accumulation of proteoglycans, associated with Marfan syndrome, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease), rheumatic disease, endocarditis, ruptured chordae.
  • Secondary (functional) regurgitation results from a dilated or ischemic ventricle that pulls the leaflets apart.
  • Acute regurgitation (papillary muscle or chordal rupture, endocarditis) causes flash pulmonary edema because a normal-sized left atrium cannot absorb the regurgitant volume.

Mitral stenosis and rheumatic heart disease

Rheumatic heart disease remains the leading cause of mitral stenosis and a major cause of heart failure in low- and middle-income countries. After group A streptococcal pharyngitis, antibodies against streptococcal antigens such as the M protein cross-react with cardiac proteins (molecular mimicry, a type II hypersensitivity). Acute carditis shows Aschoff bodies (foci of fibrinoid necrosis with lymphocytes, plasma cells and Anitschkow cells). Acute disease tends to cause mitral regurgitation; repeated attacks over years cause leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and chordal shortening, so stenosis appears decades later. The mitral valve is involved most often, then the aortic.

  • Raised left atrial pressure causes dyspnea, hemoptysis and pulmonary hypertension; the enlarged left atrium promotes atrial fibrillation and thrombus, and can compress the esophagus (dysphagia) or the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness).
  • Tachycardia shortens diastole, the time available to empty the atrium across the narrow valve, so exercise, fever, pregnancy and new atrial fibrillation provoke decompensation.
  • The higher the left atrial pressure, the sooner the valve snaps open after S2: a shorter S2–opening snap interval means more severe stenosis.

Right-sided valve disease

  • Tricuspid regurgitation: usually functional (right ventricular dilation from pulmonary hypertension or left heart disease); primary causes include endocarditis in people who inject drugs (Staphylococcus aureus), carcinoid heart disease, Ebstein anomaly and pacemaker leads.
  • Carcinoid heart disease: serotonin and other mediators from hepatic metastases of a neuroendocrine tumour reach the right heart and cause fibrous plaques that fix the tricuspid and pulmonic valves (regurgitation and stenosis). The left heart is usually spared because the lungs inactivate serotonin (monoamine oxidase).
  • Pulmonic stenosis: usually congenital (including Noonan syndrome).

Prosthetic valves

  • Mechanical valves last but need lifelong anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin).
  • Bioprosthetic valves need little long-term anticoagulation but degenerate with time (calcification and leaflet tears), sooner in younger patients.
  • Complications: valve thrombosis, thromboembolism, prosthetic valve endocarditis, paravalvular leak and intravascular hemolysis (schistocytes, raised LDH, low haptoglobin) from shear across a leak or a mechanical valve.
Stenosis → pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy (aortic stenosis). Regurgitation → volume overload → eccentric hypertrophy (aortic and mitral regurgitation). Mitral stenosis spares the left ventricle; the burden falls on the left atrium and pulmonary circulation.

s23b-s-080901-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Measuring it correctly

  • Have the patient lie supine for about 5 minutes; record pressure and pulse.
  • Stand the patient and record both at 1 and 3 minutes. A sustained fall of ≥ 20 mm Hg systolic or ≥ 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes is OH.
  • Initial OH: a large transient fall in the first 15 seconds with quick recovery; common in the young and usually benign. Delayed OH: the fall appears only after 3 minutes; a tilt-table test may be needed to show it, and it can herald autonomic failure.
  • Compare the heart-rate rise with the systolic fall. A ratio below about 0.5 beats/min per mm Hg suggests neurogenic OH, unless the patient takes a β-blocker or has a pacemaker or conduction disease.
  • Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is different: a sustained heart-rate rise of ≥ 30/min (≥ 40/min at age 12–19) within 10 minutes of standing, with symptoms, without OH; typically a young woman.

Where OH fits in the evaluation of syncope

Every patient with transient loss of consciousness gets a careful history (from witnesses too), a physical examination including orthostatic vital signs, and a 12-lead ECG. These three steps sort most patients into one of three groups:

TypeCluesNext step
Reflex (vasovagal, situational, carotid sinus)Trigger (pain, fear, prolonged standing, micturition, cough), prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating; young; normal ECGReassurance, trigger avoidance, counter-pressure manoeuvres
OrthostaticSymptoms on standing, after meals or hot showers; new antihypertensive, diuretic or α-blocker; volume loss; parkinsonism or diabetesOrthostatic vitals confirm; review drugs and volume
Cardiac (arrhythmic or structural)Syncope during exertion or lying down, sudden onset without prodrome, palpitations, known structural heart disease or low ejection fraction, family history of sudden death, abnormal ECGAdmit/monitor; echocardiogram, telemetry or ambulatory monitoring

Routine brain imaging, EEG and carotid ultrasound are low yield in syncope unless there are focal neurologic findings or suspected seizure.

Management, step by step

  1. Find and remove causes. Review every drug: stop or reduce α1 blockers, diuretics, nitrates, tricyclics, sedatives; lower antihypertensive intensity where possible. Correct volume loss, anemia and adrenal insufficiency.
  2. Non-drug measures for everyone with symptomatic OH:
    • Rise slowly in stages; sit on the edge of the bed before standing.
    • Fluid intake of about 2–3 L/day and liberal salt, unless heart failure or kidney disease prevents it; a rapid drink of about 500 mL of water raises pressure for an hour or so.
    • Waist-high compression stockings or an abdominal binder.
    • Physical counter-manoeuvres: leg crossing, squatting, calf tensing.
    • Sleep with the head of the bed raised by about 10–20° (reduces nocturnal natriuresis and supine hypertension).
    • Avoid hot environments, large carbohydrate-rich meals and alcohol; prefer small, frequent meals.
    • Reconditioning exercise, recumbent or water-based at first.
  3. Drugs when symptoms persist: midodrine (dosed during upright daytime hours), droxidopa (approved for neurogenic OH), or fludrocortisone (avoid in heart failure, hypokalemia or significant supine hypertension). Pyridostigmine is an option for mild cases.

Supine hypertension

About half of patients with neurogenic OH also have high pressure when lying down. It drives nocturnal pressure diuresis (worse OH in the morning) and end-organ damage. Manage it by avoiding the supine position during the day, raising the head of the bed at night, taking the last pressor dose at least about 4 hours before bedtime, and, if needed, a short-acting antihypertensive at bedtime only (for example, a short-acting agent such as captopril or a nitrate patch removed in the morning). Never treat supine hypertension with a long-acting daytime antihypertensive: it worsens falls.

Older adults and falls

OH in older adults is linked with falls, fractures, syncope, stroke, cognitive decline and higher mortality. A fall in an older patient should always prompt orthostatic vitals and a medication review (deprescribing). Treat to relieve symptoms and keep the patient safe, not to normalise the standing number.

The best first intervention for an older patient with new OH is almost always to stop or reduce the culprit drug, not to add a pressor.

Exertional syncope, syncope while lying down, or syncope with an abnormal ECG is not orthostatic until proven otherwise: look for aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ischemia or an arrhythmia.

s23b-s-080901-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Definition

Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is a sustained fall in systolic pressure of at least 20 mm Hg, or in diastolic pressure of at least 10 mm Hg, within 3 minutes of standing (or of head-up tilt to at least 60°). In a patient with supine hypertension, a systolic fall of 30 mm Hg is a more useful cut-off, because the fall scales with the starting pressure.

What normally happens when you stand

On standing, gravity pools about 500–800 mL of blood in the veins of the legs, buttocks and splanchnic bed. Venous return, end-diastolic volume and stroke volume fall (Frank–Starling), so arterial pressure dips for a few seconds. The arterial baroreflex corrects this:

  1. Less stretch of the carotid sinus and aortic arch lowers afferent firing (carotid sinus → glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX; aortic arch → vagus, CN X).
  2. The nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla receives less input, so vagal (parasympathetic) outflow to the heart falls and sympathetic outflow rises.
  3. Sympathetic efferents release norepinephrine: α1-mediated arteriolar and venous constriction raise resistance and venous return; β1 effects raise heart rate and contractility.
  4. Over minutes, renal sympathetic nerves and reduced renal perfusion release renin; angiotensin II and vasopressin add vasoconstriction and fluid retention.

The net effect in a healthy person: systolic pressure barely changes, diastolic pressure rises slightly, and heart rate rises by about 10–20/min. The skeletal-muscle pump of the calves also pushes blood back toward the heart.

Two mechanisms of failure

Non-neurogenic OHNeurogenic OH
ProblemToo little circulating volume, or vessels/heart that cannot respond (drugs, deconditioning)Failure of sympathetic efferent outflow, so norepinephrine is not released on standing
Heart rate on standingRises briskly (often by 20–30/min or more)Rises little: ratio of heart-rate rise to systolic fall below about 0.5 beats/min per mm Hg
ExamplesVomiting, diarrhea, bleeding, diuretics, poor intake, adrenal insufficiency, prolonged bed restParkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, dementia with Lewy bodies, pure autonomic failure, diabetic and amyloid neuropathy, spinal cord injury above T6
Plasma norepinephrine on standingRisesFails to rise appropriately

Drugs that cause or worsen OH

  • α1 antagonists (terazosin, doxazosin, prazosin; less so tamsulosin): venous and arteriolar dilation; worst with the first dose (“first-dose effect”).
  • Diuretics (volume loss), nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors (venodilation; the combination is dangerous).
  • Tricyclic antidepressants, trazodone, low-potency and some atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine, clozapine): α1 blockade.
  • Levodopa and dopamine agonists: peripheral dopaminergic vasodilation and reduced sympathetic tone.
  • Central sympatholytics (clonidine), opioids, alcohol, and sedatives.

Autonomic failure: the pathology to know

  • Parkinson disease and pure autonomic failure: α-synuclein Lewy pathology in neurons, including postganglionic sympathetic neurons (cardiac sympathetic denervation on imaging).
  • Multiple system atrophy: α-synuclein glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes; the lesion is mostly central (preganglionic), with early severe autonomic failure (OH, urinary dysfunction, erectile dysfunction), parkinsonism that responds poorly to levodopa and/or cerebellar ataxia.
  • Diabetic autonomic neuropathy: long-standing diabetes with distal sensory neuropathy, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, resting tachycardia and a fixed heart rate.
  • Amyloidosis (AL or transthyretin) infiltrates autonomic nerves; suspect it when OH accompanies neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, proteinuria or heart failure with thick ventricular walls.

Primary adrenal insufficiency causes OH through volume loss (no aldosterone → renal sodium wasting), with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation. Secondary (pituitary) insufficiency spares aldosterone, so hyperkalemia is absent.

Aging

Older adults have stiffer arteries and a less sensitive baroreflex, reduced β-adrenergic responsiveness of the heart, impaired thirst, lower renin and aldosterone, and a heart that depends more on preload (stiffer left ventricle). Add polypharmacy, and OH becomes common after age 65, especially in nursing-home residents. Postprandial hypotension (a fall within about 2 hours of a meal, from splanchnic pooling) is a related problem in the same patients.

Pharmacology of treatment

DrugMechanismKey adverse effects
MidodrineProdrug; desglymidodrine is a peripheral α1 agonist (arteriolar and venous constriction)Supine hypertension, piloerection (“goose bumps”), scalp itching, urinary retention
DroxidopaSynthetic amino acid converted directly to norepinephrine by aromatic L-amino acid (DOPA) decarboxylaseSupine hypertension, headache
FludrocortisoneMineralocorticoid-receptor agonist: renal sodium and water retention, more volumeHypokalemia, edema, heart-failure worsening, supine hypertension
PyridostigmineAcetylcholinesterase inhibitor: boosts ganglionic transmission, mostly when uprightDiarrhea, cramps, sweating; modest effect

A small heart-rate rise does not mean the patient is “fine”. When pressure falls and the pulse barely moves, think autonomic failure (or a β-blocker) rather than volume depletion.

Add polypharmacy, and OH becomes common after age 65, especially in nursing-home residents. Postprandial hypotension (a fall within about 2 hours of a meal, from splanchnic pooling) is a related problem in the same patients.

Measure it properly

Seat the patient with back supported, feet flat and arm supported at heart level, after about 5 minutes of quiet rest, with an appropriately sized cuff on bare skin; no caffeine, smoking or exercise in the previous 30 minutes. Average at least two readings on at least two occasions. Confirm the diagnosis with out-of-office readings (home monitoring or 24-hour ambulatory monitoring) whenever possible.

Category (adults)Systolic (mm Hg)Diastolic (mm Hg)
Normal< 120and< 80
Elevated120–129and< 80
Stage 1 hypertension130–139or80–89
Stage 2 hypertension≥ 140or≥ 90
  • White-coat hypertension: high office readings, normal out-of-office readings. Monitor; lifestyle advice; do not start drugs on office readings alone.
  • Masked hypertension: normal office readings, high out-of-office readings; carries risk similar to sustained hypertension.
  • A single very high reading with symptoms of organ damage is treated as an emergency, not a diagnosis to confirm later.

Initial work-up of new hypertension

Basic metabolic panel (sodium, potassium, creatinine/eGFR), fasting glucose or A1c, lipid profile, TSH, urinalysis with urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, hemoglobin, and a 12-lead ECG. These look for organ damage, cardiovascular risk factors and clues to a secondary cause (for example, unexplained hypokalemia).

Lifestyle: for everyone with elevated pressure or hypertension

  • Weight loss if overweight (roughly 1 mm Hg per kg lost).
  • A DASH-style diet: vegetables, fruit, whole grains, low-fat dairy, legumes and nuts; less saturated fat and sugar.
  • Less sodium (aim well under 2,300 mg/day, ideally about 1,500 mg) and more potassium from food (unless CKD or a potassium-raising drug makes this unsafe); potassium-enriched salt substitutes help many patients.
  • Regular aerobic and resistance exercise.
  • Limit alcohol (less is better), stop smoking, treat sleep apnea.

When to start drugs, and which

  • Stage 2: lifestyle plus drugs; most patients start two first-line agents of different classes, ideally as a single-pill combination.
  • Stage 1: drugs as well as lifestyle if the patient has clinical cardiovascular disease, diabetes, CKD or a high estimated cardiovascular risk; otherwise lifestyle for 3–6 months, then drugs if pressure stays ≥ 130/80 mm Hg.
  • Target: below 130/80 mm Hg for most adults, including older adults living in the community, if tolerated.
  • First-line classes: thiazide-type diuretic (chlorthalidone or indapamide preferred by many), ACE inhibitor or ARB, and dihydropyridine CCB.
SituationPreferred choice
Diabetes or CKD with albuminuriaACE inhibitor or ARB (not both)
Heart failure with reduced ejection fractionACE inhibitor/ARB/ARNI, evidence-based β blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor
After myocardial infarction or with anginaβ blocker plus ACE inhibitor/ARB
Black adults without CKD or heart failureThiazide-type diuretic or CCB as the initial single agent (a combination usually needed)
Pregnancy or planned pregnancyLabetalol, nifedipine (extended-release) or methyldopa; never ACE inhibitors, ARBs or direct renin inhibitors
GoutAvoid thiazides if possible; losartan lowers urate
OsteoporosisThiazide is a reasonable choice (retains calcium)

Resistant hypertension

Pressure above goal on three drugs of different classes at good doses, one being a diuretic (or needing four drugs). First exclude pseudo-resistance: poor technique, white-coat effect, non-adherence, and interfering substances (NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, oral contraceptives, high salt or alcohol). Then screen for secondary causes, especially primary aldosteronism and sleep apnea. The best-supported fourth drug is spironolactone.

Check creatinine and potassium within a few weeks of starting an ACE inhibitor, ARB or diuretic. A creatinine rise of up to about 30% is expected with RAAS blockade; a larger rise suggests renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.

When to look for a secondary cause

Onset before age 30 (especially without obesity or family history), resistant hypertension, abrupt worsening of previously controlled pressure, hypertension with unprovoked or marked diuretic-induced hypokalemia, severe hypertension or organ damage out of proportion to duration, and episodic symptoms.

CauseCluesScreening testTreatment
