Severe hypertension: emergency versus urgency

The difference is acute target-organ damage, not the number.

  • Hypertensive emergency: severe elevation (usually ≥ 180/120 mm Hg) with new organ damage: hypertensive encephalopathy, stroke, acute coronary syndrome, acute pulmonary edema, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury, retinal hemorrhages/papilledema, eclampsia, microangiopathic hemolysis. Admit to an intensive care unit and use titratable IV drugs.
  • Severe hypertension without acute organ damage (“urgency”): restart or intensify oral therapy, address triggers (pain, missed doses, drugs) and arrange follow-up within days. Rapid lowering is not needed and can be harmful.

How fast to lower

  • Most emergencies: lower pressure by no more than about 25% within the first hour, then toward 160/100–110 mm Hg over the next 2–6 hours, then to normal over 24–48 hours. Cerebral, coronary and renal autoregulation is reset upward, so abrupt normalisation causes ischemia.
  • Aortic dissection: lower heart rate first with an IV β blocker (esmolol or labetalol), then systolic pressure to about 120 mm Hg or lower within the first hour.
  • Severe preeclampsia/eclampsia and pheochromocytoma crisis: lower systolic pressure below about 140 mm Hg in the first hour.
  • Acute ischemic stroke: permissive hypertension unless thrombolysis is planned (then below 185/110 mm Hg before and below 180/105 mm Hg for 24 hours after).

Sublingual or rapid-release oral nifedipine causes unpredictable precipitous falls in pressure, stroke and MI. It has no role in hypertensive urgency or emergency.

s23b-s-081001-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Pressure, flow and resistance

Mean arterial pressure = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance (+ central venous pressure, usually ignored). Long-term pressure is set by the kidney: at any given pressure, the kidney excretes salt and water until intake equals output (pressure natriuresis). Almost every form of sustained hypertension involves a shift of this relation so that balance is reached only at a higher pressure.

Essential (primary) hypertension

About 90% of adult hypertension has no single identifiable cause. Contributors include genetics, high sodium and low potassium intake, obesity and insulin resistance, physical inactivity, alcohol, sympathetic overactivity, arterial stiffening with age, and reduced nephron number. Hypertension is more common and starts earlier in Black adults in the United States, a pattern driven by social and environmental as well as biological factors.

The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS)

  • Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole in response to low renal perfusion pressure, β1 sympathetic stimulation, and low NaCl delivery sensed by the macula densa.
  • Renin cleaves angiotensinogen (liver) to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme (mostly pulmonary endothelium) makes angiotensin II and also degrades bradykinin.
  • Angiotensin II (AT1 receptor): arteriolar vasoconstriction, efferent arteriolar constriction (preserves GFR when renal perfusion falls), aldosterone release from the zona glomerulosa, proximal tubule Na+/H+ exchange, ADH release and thirst, and cardiac and vascular remodelling.
  • Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the collecting duct: more ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase, so Na+ is reabsorbed and K+ (and, via intercalated cells, H+) is secreted.

Pathology of sustained hypertension

LesionSettingAppearanceConsequence
Hyaline arteriolosclerosisLong-standing benign hypertension, diabetes, agingHomogeneous pink thickening of arteriolar walls from plasma protein leakage and matrixBenign nephrosclerosis: small, finely granular kidneys; slow CKD
Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosisSevere (malignant) hypertensionConcentric, laminated “onion-skin” smooth-muscle and basement-membrane layers, often with fibrinoid necrosisMalignant nephrosclerosis: acute kidney injury, “flea-bitten” kidney with petechial hemorrhages
  • Heart: concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in parallel), diastolic dysfunction, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, coronary disease.
  • Brain: lacunar infarcts; Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms of lenticulostriate arteries → intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons and cerebellum.
  • Aorta: hypertension is the main risk factor for aortic dissection; also abdominal aortic aneurysm (with smoking).
  • Eye: arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, papilledema in malignant hypertension.

Drug mechanisms and adverse effects

ClassMechanismAdverse effects to know
Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide)Block the Na+–Cl− cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule; long-term vasodilationHypokalemia, hyponatremia, metabolic alkalosis, hypercalcemia (less urinary Ca2+), hyperuricemia/gout, hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia
ACE inhibitors (-pril)Block angiotensin II formation and bradykinin breakdownDry cough and angioedema (bradykinin), hyperkalemia, AKI in bilateral renal artery stenosis, teratogenic (fetal renal damage)
Angiotensin receptor blockers (-sartan)Block AT1 receptorsAs ACE inhibitors but cough is rare; teratogenic; never combine with an ACE inhibitor
Dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine)Block L-type Ca2+ channels in vascular smooth muscle (arteriolar dilation)Ankle edema, flushing, headache, reflex tachycardia, gingival hyperplasia
Mineralocorticoid antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone)Block aldosterone receptorsHyperkalemia; gynecomastia and menstrual changes with spironolactone (androgen-receptor effects)
β blockersLower heart rate, contractility and renin releaseBradycardia, fatigue; not first-line without a specific indication
HydralazineDirect arteriolar dilator (increases cGMP)Reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, drug-induced lupus
MinoxidilOpens KATP channels in arteriolar smooth muscleHypertrichosis, marked fluid retention, pericardial effusion
ClonidineCentral α2 agonistSedation, dry mouth, rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly

Why does ACE inhibition cause AKI in bilateral renal artery stenosis? Glomerular filtration in a poorly perfused kidney depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. Remove it and glomerular pressure collapses.

Primary aldosteronism and renovascular hypertension both cause hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, but renin is low in primary aldosteronism and high in renovascular disease.

s23b-s-081101-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Screening and testing

  • A lipid panel (total cholesterol, HDL, triglyceride, calculated or measured LDL; non-fasting is acceptable for most adults) is part of cardiovascular risk assessment in adults. Children are screened universally once at about 9–11 years and again at 17–21 years, and earlier if there is a family history of premature cardiovascular disease or severe hypercholesterolemia.
  • Exclude secondary causes before labelling dyslipidemia primary: hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestatic liver disease (high LDL); uncontrolled diabetes, obesity, alcohol, CKD, estrogen therapy, glucocorticoids, retinoids, antiretrovirals, atypical antipsychotics, thiazides and β blockers (high triglyceride).
  • Many guidelines now advise measuring lipoprotein(a) at least once in adulthood; apoB and coronary artery calcium scoring help when the decision to treat is uncertain.

Who gets a statin

GroupTherapy
Clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ACS, MI, stable angina, coronary or other arterial revascularization, ischemic stroke/TIA, symptomatic peripheral artery disease)High-intensity statin; add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor if LDL stays above goal
LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL (age 20–75)High-intensity statin without needing a risk calculation; evaluate for familial hypercholesterolemia and test first-degree relatives
Diabetes, age 40–75At least moderate-intensity statin; high-intensity if other risk factors or target-organ damage
Primary prevention, age 40–75, without diabetesShared decision guided by estimated 10-year risk, risk enhancers (family history, Lp(a), CKD, inflammatory disease, South Asian ancestry, premature menopause, preeclampsia history) and, if uncertain, coronary calcium score
IntensityLDL loweringExamples
High≥ 50%Atorvastatin 40–80 mg, rosuvastatin 20–40 mg
Moderate30–49%Atorvastatin 10–20 mg, rosuvastatin 5–10 mg, simvastatin 20–40 mg, pravastatin 40–80 mg
Low< 30%Simvastatin 10 mg, pravastatin 10–20 mg

Recheck a lipid panel 4–12 weeks after starting or changing therapy, then every 3–12 months as needed, to check adherence and response.

Adding non-statin therapy

  1. Confirm adherence and maximise statin intensity.
  2. Add ezetimibe (oral, cheap, about 20% further LDL lowering).
  3. Add a PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab or alirocumab; inclisiran is an alternative) for very-high-risk patients or familial hypercholesterolemia with LDL still above goal. These reduce cardiovascular events.
  4. Bempedoic acid for patients who cannot take adequate statin doses; it reduced events in statin-intolerant patients.

Statin-associated muscle symptoms

  • Most muscle aches on statins are not caused by the drug. With tolerable symptoms and a normal or mildly raised CK: stop the statin until symptoms resolve, then rechallenge with the same statin at a lower dose, a different statin, or alternate-day dosing. Check TSH (hypothyroidism predisposes) and review interacting drugs.
  • CK more than 10 times the upper limit, myoglobinuria or acute kidney injury means rhabdomyolysis: stop the statin and give IV fluids.
  • Rare statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (anti-HMG-CoA reductase antibodies) persists after stopping the drug and needs immunosuppression.
  • Routine CK and transaminase monitoring is not needed; check a baseline ALT and recheck only for symptoms.

Hypertriglyceridemia

  • Treat secondary causes first: alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes, obesity, hypothyroidism, offending drugs.
  • Lifestyle: weight loss, cut alcohol, refined carbohydrates and sugar-sweetened drinks, regular exercise.
  • Triglyceride ≥ about 1,000 mg/dL (or ≥ 500 mg/dL with other risks): the goal is to prevent pancreatitis. Start a fibrate (fenofibrate) and, for chylomicronemia, a very-low-fat diet; prescription omega-3 fatty acids can be added.
  • Moderate hypertriglyceridemia in a patient with ASCVD (or diabetes plus risk factors) already on a statin: icosapent ethyl (purified EPA) reduces cardiovascular events; mixed EPA/DHA supplements have not.
  • Familial chylomicronemia (LPL deficiency): dietary fat restricted to about 10–15% of calories (fibrates work poorly because LPL is absent); medium-chain triglycerides are absorbed directly into portal blood and can be used.

Nutrition

For LDL lowering, replace saturated and trans fats with unsaturated fats (olive and canola oils, nuts, fish), increase soluble fibre (oats, legumes) and choose a Mediterranean or DASH-style pattern. Dietary cholesterol matters less than saturated fat for most people. Statins are usually stopped before conception and during pregnancy and breastfeeding, except in very-high-risk patients after specialist advice.

LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL is treated with a high-intensity statin regardless of calculated risk. Do not wait for a risk score or calcium scan.

LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL is treated with a high-intensity statin regardless of calculated risk. Do not wait for a risk score or calcium scan.

s23b-s-081201-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Suspected acute aortic dissection

Consider dissection in anyone with abrupt, severe chest, back or abdominal pain, especially with hypertension, a pulse or blood pressure difference between limbs, a focal neurological deficit, syncope, a new aortic regurgitation murmur or a known connective-tissue disorder. Pain with neurological signs or limb ischemia is a strong pointer.

Imaging

  • Hemodynamically stable: CT angiography of the chest (often chest, abdomen and pelvis) is the usual first test: fast, widely available and shows extent and malperfusion.
  • Unstable, or cannot go to the scanner: transesophageal echocardiography at the bedside or in the operating room. Bedside transthoracic echo may show pericardial effusion, aortic regurgitation or a flap in the root but cannot exclude dissection.
  • MR angiography is accurate but slow; useful for follow-up and in stable patients who cannot have contrast CT.
  • A chest radiograph may show a wide mediastinum but is normal in a meaningful share of cases, so it never rules dissection out.

Initial medical therapy (both types)

  1. Analgesia (intravenous opioid): pain drives catecholamines.
  2. An intravenous beta-blocker first (esmolol, labetalol or metoprolol) to lower heart rate (target about 60/min or less) and the force of ejection. If beta-blockers cannot be used, a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is the alternative.
  3. Then, if systolic pressure is still high, add a vasodilator (for example nitroprusside or nicardipine) aiming for the lowest pressure that keeps organs perfused, typically systolic 100–120 mm Hg.

A vasodilator given before rate control causes reflex tachycardia and increases shear on the flap. Anticoagulants, antiplatelet drugs and fibrinolytics are harmful in dissection, which is why it must be excluded before treating a suspected STEMI with severe back pain.

Definitive treatment

TypeManagement
Type A (ascending)Emergency open surgical repair. Mortality without surgery rises by the hour, mainly from tamponade, rupture, coronary occlusion and severe aortic regurgitation. Do not attempt pericardiocentesis for tamponade except as a bridge in arrest.
Type B, uncomplicatedMedical therapy (rate and pressure control), monitoring and serial imaging.
Type B, complicatedMalperfusion (gut, kidney, limb), rupture, rapid expansion or refractory pain or hypertension: endovascular stent-graft repair (TEVAR).

Long term: lifelong blood-pressure control with a beta-blocker as part of the regimen, imaging surveillance, and avoidance of heavy isometric exercise. Screen first-degree relatives when an inherited aortopathy is suspected.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm

Screening

A one-time abdominal ultrasound is recommended for men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked (USPSTF). It is selectively offered to men in that age group who never smoked; it is not recommended for women who never smoked.

Surveillance and repair

  • Small aneurysms are watched with periodic ultrasound; intervals shorten as the diameter grows (roughly every few years for 3.0–3.9 cm and about yearly for 4.0–4.9 cm).
  • Elective repair is generally offered at a diameter of about 5.5 cm in men (about 5.0 cm in women, whose aneurysms rupture at smaller sizes), with rapid growth (about 0.5 cm or more in a year), or when the aneurysm causes symptoms such as tenderness or pain.
  • Open or endovascular repair (EVAR) depends on anatomy and fitness; EVAR has lower early mortality and needs lifelong imaging for endoleak.
  • Meanwhile: stop smoking (the single most effective way to slow growth), treat blood pressure, and give a statin and antiplatelet therapy for the accompanying atherosclerotic risk.

Rupture

Sudden abdominal or back pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass in an older smoker is a ruptured AAA until proven otherwise. An unstable patient goes straight to the operating room (or the endovascular suite); a stable patient with suspected leak can have a rapid CT angiogram. Use permissive hypotension (enough pressure to keep the patient alert) rather than aggressive fluids before control of bleeding. Rupture can mimic renal colic or diverticulitis; consider it in any older patient with "renal colic" and hypotension.

Contained retroperitoneal rupture can present as flank pain with ecchymosis and only transient hypotension. An inflammatory aneurysm or aortoenteric fistula (after graft repair: a herald gastrointestinal bleed) are less common but testable twists.

Superior vena cava syndrome

Confirm with contrast CT of the chest. If no tissue diagnosis exists, obtain one before giving steroids or radiation, because both can obscure lymphoma histology, unless there is airway compromise or cerebral edema, which call for urgent endovascular stenting. Treat the cause (chemotherapy for small cell lung cancer or lymphoma, radiation for other tumors); catheter-related thrombosis needs anticoagulation and often catheter removal. Elevate the head of the bed meanwhile.

s23b-s-081202-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Diagnosis of peripheral artery disease

  • Suspect PAD with exertional leg pain, non-healing foot wounds, abnormal pulses or a femoral bruit, especially in smokers, people with diabetes or kidney disease and those over 65.
  • Resting ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the first test: ≤ 0.90 diagnoses PAD, 0.91–0.99 is borderline, 1.00–1.40 is normal, and > 1.40 means noncompressible (calcified) arteries.
  • Normal or borderline resting ABI with typical symptoms → exercise ABI (a fall after treadmill walking).
  • ABI > 1.40 (common in diabetes and chronic kidney disease) → toe-brachial index (digital arteries are rarely calcified) or other physiological testing.
  • Anatomical imaging (duplex ultrasound, CT or MR angiography, catheter angiography) is for planning revascularization, not for making the diagnosis.

Management of chronic symptomatic PAD

  1. Risk reduction for everyone: stop smoking (the most important step), high-intensity statin, single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel), blood pressure and glucose control, foot care. In selected patients at high ischemic and low bleeding risk, low-dose rivaroxaban added to aspirin reduces major cardiovascular and limb events. ACE inhibitors or ARBs for hypertension.
  2. Claudication: a supervised exercise program (walking to moderate pain, rest, repeat; about three sessions a week for at least 12 weeks) is first-line and improves walking distance more than most drugs. Cilostazol can be added if symptoms still limit life, but never in heart failure.
  3. Revascularization (endovascular or bypass) for lifestyle-limiting claudication despite exercise and medication, and for chronic limb-threatening ischemia.

Chronic limb-threatening ischemia

Ischemic rest pain, non-healing ulcers or gangrene for more than 2 weeks. High risk of amputation and death. Needs prompt anatomical imaging and revascularization, wound care and infection control. Amputation is reserved for non-salvageable limbs.

Acute limb ischemia

A sudden fall in limb perfusion threatening viability, from embolism (usually from the heart in atrial fibrillation or after myocardial infarction; abrupt onset, normal pulses in the other leg) or thrombosis of a diseased artery or bypass graft (history of claudication). Look for the six Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia (cold), paresthesia and paralysis. Sensory loss and weakness mean the limb is threatened.

  1. Give an intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion immediately to stop clot propagation, unless contraindicated.
  2. Assess viability: sensation, motor function and Doppler signals.
  3. Viable or marginally threatened: urgent imaging, then catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgery. Immediately threatened (sensory loss beyond the toes, weakness): emergency revascularization (embolectomy or bypass). Irreversible (profound paralysis, no Doppler signals): amputation.
  4. After reperfusion watch for compartment syndrome (pain on passive stretch, tense calf; treat with fasciotomy), hyperkalemia, myoglobinuria and acidosis.
  5. Find and treat the source (ECG, echocardiography); long-term anticoagulation after embolism from atrial fibrillation.

Carotid artery stenosis

  • Symptomatic (TIA or non-disabling stroke in the territory within the past 6 months) with 70–99% stenosis: carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks. Moderate stenosis (50–69%) may benefit depending on patient factors. Stenting is an alternative when surgical risk is high. Near-occlusion and complete occlusion are not operated on.
  • Everyone: antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, blood pressure control and smoking cessation.
  • Do not screen asymptomatic adults for carotid stenosis.

Mesenteric ischemia (arterial)

Chronic mesenteric ischemia: postprandial abdominal pain beginning 15–60 minutes after eating, fear of food and weight loss in an older smoker with vascular disease; diagnose with CT angiography and revascularize. Acute mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion to examination (often embolic in atrial fibrillation); urgent CT angiography, heparin and revascularization, with resection of dead bowel.

Cholesterol embolization and Raynaud phenomenon

Atheroemboli are managed supportively: statin, blood pressure control, avoidance of further instrumentation and of new anticoagulation where possible. For Raynaud, keep the whole body warm, stop smoking and avoid triggers; a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (such as nifedipine or amlodipine) is first-line drug therapy. Evaluate suspected secondary Raynaud with antinuclear antibodies and nailfold capillaroscopy.

s23b-s-081203-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Diagnosing deep vein thrombosis

Symptoms: unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth and dilated superficial veins; calf circumference difference of 3 cm or more is significant. Clinical findings alone are unreliable, so use a structured pretest probability (the Wells score) and then:

  • DVT unlikely (low pretest probability): high-sensitivity D-dimer. Negative → DVT excluded. Positive → compression ultrasound.
  • DVT likely: go straight to compression ultrasound of the proximal veins (or whole leg). D-dimer cannot rule out DVT here.
  • D-dimer is less useful in pregnancy, after surgery, in cancer, in older adults and in inpatients because it is often raised; go to imaging.
  • Suspected iliac or caval thrombosis with normal leg ultrasound: CT or MR venography.

Treatment of DVT

  1. Anticoagulate. If suspicion is high and the test will be delayed, start anticoagulation while waiting (absent high bleeding risk).
  2. Choose the drug:
    • Most patients: a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban or rivaroxaban can be started without heparin; dabigatran and edoxaban follow at least 5 days of parenteral anticoagulation). DOACs are preferred over warfarin for most patients.
    • Cancer-associated VTE: a DOAC (apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) or low-molecular-weight heparin. LMWH or apixaban may be favored with luminal gastrointestinal or genitourinary cancers because of bleeding risk with some DOACs.
    • Pregnancy: LMWH (warfarin is teratogenic; DOACs cross the placenta and are avoided).
    • Antiphospholipid syndrome (especially triple positive) and mechanical heart valves: warfarin, not a DOAC.
    • Severe renal impairment: unfractionated heparin or warfarin are safer choices than renally cleared agents.
    • Warfarin, if used, overlaps with heparin for at least 5 days and until the INR is 2–3 for 24 hours (target INR 2.5).
  3. Duration: provoked by a major transient risk factor (surgery, major trauma, immobilizing illness) → 3 months. Unprovoked or with a persistent risk factor (active cancer) → at least 3 months, then often indefinite if bleeding risk allows, with periodic review. Recurrent unprovoked VTE → indefinite.
  4. IVC filter: only for acute proximal DVT or PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (for example active bleeding or recent intracranial hemorrhage); start anticoagulation and consider filter removal once it becomes safe.
  5. Isolated distal (calf) DVT without severe symptoms or risk factors for extension: serial ultrasound over 2 weeks is an alternative to anticoagulation.

Massive iliofemoral DVT can obstruct nearly all venous outflow: a swollen, painful, cyanotic leg (phlegmasia cerulea dolens) that can progress to venous gangrene and compromise arterial inflow. Treat with anticoagulation, elevation and urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy. May-Thurner syndrome (compression of the left iliac vein by the right iliac artery) explains left-sided iliofemoral DVT in younger women.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Suspect when platelets fall by more than 50% (or a new thrombosis occurs) 5–10 days after heparin is started. Estimate probability with the 4Ts score (degree of thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis, other causes). If intermediate or high probability: stop all heparin (including flushes and LMWH) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC; send a PF4 immunoassay and, if positive, a functional assay. Do not start warfarin until platelets recover (it can cause venous limb gangrene), and avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding.

VTE prevention in hospital

  • Acutely ill medical patients at increased risk and low bleeding risk: subcutaneous LMWH, unfractionated heparin or fondaparinux.
  • High bleeding risk: mechanical prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression).
  • Major orthopedic surgery (hip or knee arthroplasty, hip fracture): pharmacological prophylaxis (LMWH, a DOAC or aspirin in selected arthroplasty patients) for weeks after surgery.
  • Early mobilization for everyone.

Superficial vein thrombosis

  • A short segment (for example at an old IV site in the arm): warm compresses, NSAIDs, elevation; remove any catheter.
  • Leg superficial thrombosis of 5 cm or more: prophylactic-dose anticoagulation (for example fondaparinux for about 45 days).
  • Within about 3 cm of the saphenofemoral junction: treat as a DVT.
  • Recurrent migratory thrombophlebitis without a clear cause: look for cancer (Trousseau syndrome) and Buerger disease in young smokers.

Chronic venous disease

Compression therapy (graded stockings, multilayer bandages for ulcers), leg elevation, exercise and weight loss are the basis. Venous ulcers heal with compression plus local wound care; check the ABI first because compression is unsafe with significant arterial disease. Symptomatic varicose veins with reflux are treated with endovenous thermal ablation, sclerotherapy or surgery. Post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic pain, swelling and ulcers after DVT) is managed the same way.

only for acute proximal DVT or PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (for example active bleeding or recent intracranial hemorrhage); start anticoagulation and consider filter removal once it becomes safe.
without severe symptoms or risk factors for extension: serial ultrasound over 2 weeks is an alternative to anticoagulation.
Massive iliofemoral DVT can obstruct nearly all venous outflow: a swollen, painful, cyanotic leg (

) that can progress to venous gangrene and compromise arterial inflow. Treat with anticoagulation, elevation and urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy. May-Thurner syndrome (compression of the left iliac vein by the right iliac artery) explains left-sided iliofemoral DVT in younger women.

Suspect when platelets fall by more than 50% (or a new thrombosis occurs) 5–10 days after heparin is started. Estimate probability with the 4Ts score (degree of thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis, other causes). If intermediate or high probability:

(including flushes and LMWH) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC; send a PF4 immunoassay and, if positive, a functional assay. Do not start warfarin until platelets recover (it can cause venous limb gangrene), and avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding.
Acutely ill medical patients at increased risk and low bleeding risk: subcutaneous LMWH, unfractionated heparin or fondaparinux.
High bleeding risk: mechanical prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression).
Major orthopedic surgery (hip or knee arthroplasty, hip fracture): pharmacological prophylaxis (LMWH, a DOAC or aspirin in selected arthroplasty patients) for weeks after surgery.
A short segment (for example at an old IV site in the arm): warm compresses, NSAIDs, elevation; remove any catheter.
Leg superficial thrombosis of 5 cm or more: prophylactic-dose anticoagulation (for example fondaparinux for about 45 days).
Within about 3 cm of the saphenofemoral junction: treat as a DVT.
Recurrent migratory thrombophlebitis without a clear cause: look for cancer (Trousseau syndrome) and Buerger disease in young smokers.

Compression therapy (graded stockings, multilayer bandages for ulcers), leg elevation, exercise and weight loss are the basis. Venous ulcers heal with compression plus local wound care; check the ABI first because compression is unsafe with significant arterial disease. Symptomatic varicose veins with reflux are treated with endovenous thermal ablation, sclerotherapy or surgery. Post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic pain, swelling and ulcers after DVT) is managed the same way.

s23b-s-081201-s1-01.bodyHtml:
The aorta is an elastic artery. Its media is built from concentric elastic lamellae, smooth muscle cells and ground substance, and it is nourished in its outer part by the vasa vasorum. Almost every disease of the great vessels tested on Step 1 is a failure of that media: it either weakens and balloons (aneurysm) or splits (dissection).

Wall stress and why big aneurysms grow faster

By the law of Laplace, wall tension rises with pressure × radius and falls with wall thickness. A dilated segment therefore carries more tension than its normal neighbours, which stretches it further: a positive feedback loop. This is why rupture risk climbs steeply with diameter and why lowering blood pressure and the rate of pressure rise (dP/dt) is the basis of medical therapy.

Aortic dissection

An intimal tear lets blood under pressure enter the media and track along it, creating a false lumen separated from the true lumen by an intimal–medial flap. The underlying lesion is usually medial degeneration, and the main driver is chronic hypertension, present in most patients.

FeatureStanford type AStanford type B
SegmentInvolves the ascending aorta (may extend distally)Begins beyond the left subclavian artery; ascending aorta spared
Typical deadly complicationsRupture into the pericardium (tamponade), acute aortic regurgitation, coronary ostial occlusion (most often the right coronary), strokeVisceral, renal or limb malperfusion; rupture
Usual treatmentEmergency surgeryMedical therapy; endovascular repair if complicated

Risk factors beyond hypertension: inherited connective-tissue disorders (Marfan syndrome, vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), a bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, Turner syndrome, stimulant use (cocaine, amphetamines), late pregnancy and the peripartum period, prior cardiac surgery or catheterization, and blunt deceleration trauma.

Classic picture: sudden, maximal-at-onset tearing or ripping pain in the chest that moves to the back, with a pulse or systolic pressure difference between the arms and a widened mediastinum on chest radiograph. A new diastolic murmur means the dissection has reached the aortic root.

Inferior ST elevation plus severe back pain: think of a type A dissection occluding the right coronary ostium before reaching for fibrinolysis or heparin.

Histology: cystic medial degeneration

The characteristic lesion is fragmentation and loss of elastic fibers with pools of basophilic, mucoid ground substance in the media and loss of smooth muscle cells (older term: cystic medial necrosis, although there is no true necrosis). It appears with ageing and hypertension and early in inherited aortopathies.

Inherited aortopathies

DisorderDefectVascular pictureClues
Marfan syndromeFBN1 (fibrillin-1), autosomal dominant; abnormal microfibrils also release excess TGF-β signallingAortic root dilation, dissection, aortic and mitral regurgitation, mitral valve prolapseTall with long limbs, arachnodactyly, upward lens dislocation, pectus deformity
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndromeCOL3A1 (type III collagen), autosomal dominantRupture or dissection of medium and large arteries, often without prior dilation; bowel and uterine ruptureThin translucent skin, easy bruising, less joint laxity than other types
Loeys-Dietz syndromeTGF-β receptor pathway genesAggressive aneurysms anywhere, arterial tortuosityBifid uvula, widely spaced eyes

Thoracic aortic aneurysm

Ascending aneurysms are mainly due to medial degeneration (age, hypertension, bicuspid valve, inherited disorders). An expanding aneurysm compresses neighbours: the airway (cough, stridor), the esophagus (dysphagia) or the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum (hoarseness). Root dilation stretches the valve annulus and causes aortic regurgitation.

Tertiary syphilis (now rare) inflames the vasa vasorum: an obliterative endarteritis with plasma cells starves the outer media, which scars and weakens. The thoracic aorta, especially the ascending part and arch, dilates; the intima looks wrinkled like tree bark, and the root can dilate enough to cause aortic regurgitation.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)

Most AAAs lie below the renal arteries. They are linked to atherosclerosis, but the defining process is chronic transmural inflammation with matrix metalloproteinases from macrophages degrading elastin and collagen in the media. Risk factors: smoking (the strongest modifiable one), age, male sex, family history, hypertension and other atherosclerotic disease. Diabetes is, interestingly, associated with lower risk. Most AAAs are silent; rupture presents with abdominal, back or flank pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass.

Superior vena cava syndrome

Obstruction of the SVC, usually by a mediastinal malignancy (lung cancer, especially small cell, or lymphoma) and increasingly by thrombus around catheters or device leads. Venous pressure rises in the head, neck and arms: facial and arm swelling, a sense of fullness worse on bending forward, distended neck and chest-wall veins (collaterals, including through the azygos system), and sometimes headache from raised intracranial venous pressure.

s23b-s-081202-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Three kinds of arteriosclerosis

TypeVesselsLesionAssociations
AtherosclerosisElastic and large-to-medium muscular arteries (abdominal aorta, coronaries, popliteal, internal carotid, circle of Willis)Intimal plaque: lipid core, foam cells, fibrous capIschemic heart disease, stroke, PAD, AAA
Arteriolosclerosis, hyalineSmall arteries and arteriolesHomogeneous pink thickening from leaked plasma proteins and excess basement-membrane matrix; narrowed lumenBenign (chronic) hypertension, diabetes, ageing → nephrosclerosis
Arteriolosclerosis, hyperplasticArteriolesConcentric "onion-skin" layers of smooth muscle and reduplicated basement membrane, sometimes fibrinoid necrosisSevere (malignant) hypertension
Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosisMedium-sized muscular arteries (femoral, tibial, radial, uterine)Ring-like calcification of the internal elastic lamina and media; lumen not narrowedAge over 50, diabetes, chronic kidney disease; "pipe-stem" arteries on radiographs, falsely high ankle pressures

Atherogenesis step by step

  1. Endothelial dysfunction from hypertension, smoking, hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia and disturbed flow at branch points: more permeability and more adhesion molecules (such as VCAM-1).
  2. Lipoprotein entry and oxidation: LDL accumulates in the intima and is oxidized.
  3. Monocyte recruitment: monocytes adhere, migrate and become macrophages that take up oxidized LDL through scavenger receptors, becoming foam cells. Collections of foam cells form the fatty streak, the earliest visible lesion (present even in adolescents).
  4. Smooth muscle migration and proliferation: growth factors such as PDGF from platelets, macrophages and endothelium draw smooth muscle cells from the media into the intima, where they make collagen and form the fibrous cap.
  5. Mature plaque: a necrotic core of lipid, cholesterol crystals and debris under the cap, with calcification and neovascularization.
  6. Complications: rupture or erosion of the cap (thin caps with many macrophages are "vulnerable") exposes thrombogenic contents → thrombosis; hemorrhage into the plaque; embolism of plaque contents; weakening of the underlying media → aneurysm.

Stable plaques with thick caps cause gradual narrowing and exertional symptoms (angina, claudication). Unstable plaques rupture and cause acute events (myocardial infarction, stroke, acute limb ischemia) often at only moderate stenosis.

Peripheral artery disease (PAD)

Atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries to the legs. Resistance in a tube rises with the fourth power of the falling radius (Poiseuille), so a stenosis that is trivial at rest becomes limiting when exercise lowers downstream resistance and flow should rise. Calf muscles then become ischemic: claudication, a cramping pain that appears reproducibly with walking and settles within minutes of standing still. The level of pain points to the level of disease: buttock and thigh (aorto-iliac; with erectile dysfunction and absent femoral pulses this is Leriche syndrome), calf (femoro-popliteal, the commonest).

Severe disease reduces flow even at rest: pain in the forefoot at night relieved by hanging the leg down, non-healing ulcers and gangrene. Signs: weak pulses, cool shiny hairless skin, thick nails, dependent rubor and pallor on elevation.

Drugs used in PAD

DrugMechanismNotes
AspirinIrreversible COX-1 acetylation → less platelet thromboxane A2Lowers cardiovascular events
ClopidogrelProdrug; active metabolite irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptorActivated by CYP2C19: poor metabolizers get less effect
CilostazolPhosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor → ↑ cAMP in platelets (less aggregation) and vascular smooth muscle (vasodilation)Improves walking distance; contraindicated in heart failure; headache, palpitations, diarrhea
StatinsHMG-CoA reductase inhibition; plaque stabilizationIndicated for all patients with PAD

Other arterial disorders of the limbs

  • Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease): segmental, thrombosing inflammation of small and medium arteries and veins of the hands and feet in young heavy smokers (usually under 45). Distal ischemia, digital ulcers, superficial migratory thrombophlebitis and Raynaud phenomenon. Only stopping all tobacco halts it.
  • Raynaud phenomenon: exaggerated vasospasm of digital arteries with cold or stress; fingers turn white (ischemia), blue (deoxygenation) then red (reactive hyperemia). Primary Raynaud is common in young women, symmetric, without ulcers. Secondary Raynaud accompanies systemic sclerosis, lupus, other connective-tissue diseases, vibrating tools and some drugs; suspect it with onset after 40, asymmetry, digital ulcers or abnormal nailfold capillaries.
  • Cholesterol (atheroembolic) embolization: showers of cholesterol crystals from aortic plaques, often after catheterization, vascular surgery or anticoagulation. Livedo reticularis, blue toes with palpable pulses, acute kidney injury, transient eosinophilia and low complement. Biopsy: biconvex, needle-shaped clefts (crystals dissolved in processing) in small arteries.
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia: non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory thickening (most often of the media) of medium arteries, especially renal and internal carotid, typically in women aged 20–60. Angiography shows a "string of beads". Renal artery involvement causes renovascular hypertension with high renin.

Mönckeberg sclerosis does not narrow the lumen but makes arteries incompressible, so the ankle-brachial index can read falsely high even when atherosclerosis coexists.

s23b-s-081203-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Why veins clot: the Virchow triad

ElementExamples
StasisImmobility, long travel, paralysis, casts, heart failure, pregnancy (compression of pelvic veins), venous obstruction
Endothelial injurySurgery (especially hip/knee replacement and hip fracture), trauma, central venous catheters, prior DVT
HypercoagulabilityCancer, estrogen (pregnancy, postpartum, combined contraceptives, hormone therapy), nephrotic syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, inherited thrombophilias

Deep vein thrombi usually start in the valve pockets of the calf veins, where flow is slow, and may propagate into the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins. Proximal thrombi are the ones most likely to embolize to the lungs. Venous thrombi are red (rich in red cells and fibrin), unlike platelet-rich arterial thrombi; that is why anticoagulants, not antiplatelet drugs, are the mainstay of treatment.

Inherited thrombophilias

DisorderMechanismNotes
Factor V LeidenPoint mutation (Arg506Gln) at the activated-protein-C cleavage site; factor Va resists inactivationMost common inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry
Prothrombin G20210AMutation in the 3′ untranslated region raises prothrombin levelsVenous thrombosis; second most common
Protein C or S deficiencyLess inactivation of factors Va and VIIIaWarfarin-induced skin necrosis when warfarin is started without heparin cover
Antithrombin deficiencyLess inhibition of thrombin and XaReduced response to heparin (heparin works through antithrombin)

Acquired look-alikes: antiphospholipid syndrome (venous and arterial clots, pregnancy loss, a prolonged aPTT that does not correct with mixing) and Trousseau syndrome, migratory superficial thrombophlebitis that can herald a visceral adenocarcinoma, classically of the pancreas.

Anticoagulant pharmacology

DrugMechanismMonitoringReversal
Unfractionated heparinBinds antithrombin and greatly accelerates its inhibition of thrombin (IIa) and XaaPTT or anti-Xa levelProtamine sulfate
Low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin)Antithrombin-mediated, mainly anti-Xa (chains too short to bridge thrombin)Usually none; anti-Xa in renal failure, pregnancy, extremes of weightProtamine (partial)
FondaparinuxSynthetic pentasaccharide; antithrombin-mediated Xa inhibition onlyNoneNo specific agent
WarfarinInhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) → fewer γ-carboxylated factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C, SPT/INRVitamin K; four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate for serious bleeding
Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxabanDirect factor Xa inhibitorsNone routinelyAndexanet alfa (a decoy Xa); prothrombin complex concentrate
DabigatranOral direct thrombin inhibitorNone routinelyIdarucizumab (antibody fragment); dialysable
Argatroban, bivalirudinParenteral direct thrombin inhibitorsaPTTNone specific

Warfarin's slow onset: existing factors must decay first. Factor VII and protein C have the shortest half-lives, so the INR rises early while protein C falls before the long-lived prothrombin. For the first days warfarin can be pro-thrombotic, which is why VTE treatment overlaps it with heparin for at least 5 days and until the INR is therapeutic, and why protein C deficiency predisposes to warfarin skin necrosis.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

An immune reaction: IgG antibodies bind complexes of heparin and platelet factor 4 (PF4) on platelets; the Fc parts cross-link platelet FcγRIIa receptors, activating platelets, releasing procoagulant microparticles and removing platelets. The result is a fall in platelets of more than 50% typically 5–10 days after starting heparin (sooner with recent exposure) and, paradoxically, venous and arterial thrombosis. It is more common with unfractionated than low-molecular-weight heparin.

Varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency

Incompetent valves in superficial veins (or after DVT damages deep valves) let blood reflux, raising venous pressure in the lower leg when standing. Superficial veins dilate and become tortuous. Chronic venous hypertension pushes red cells and fluid into tissue: edema, brown hemosiderin pigmentation, stasis dermatitis, fibrosis of fat (lipodermatosclerosis) and finally ulcers, typically above the medial malleolus. Risk factors: age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, prolonged standing, family history.

Venous ulcers: medial malleolus, shallow, irregular, with surrounding pigmentation and good pulses. Arterial ulcers: toes and pressure points, punched-out, painful, with absent pulses. Neuropathic ulcers: plantar pressure points, painless.

s23b-s-081301-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Primary survey first

Airway, breathing and circulation come first. Obstructive causes of shock in chest trauma (tension pneumothorax and tamponade) are treated as soon as they are recognised, before imaging beyond the bedside. Bedside ultrasound (extended FAST) looks at the pericardium, both pleural spaces and the abdomen in about a minute.

Penetrating cardiac injury

  • Unstable, pericardial blood on ultrasound: immediate operation (median sternotomy or anterolateral thoracotomy) to relieve tamponade and repair the wound.
  • Pericardiocentesis is only a temporising step when no surgeon or operating room is available: clotted blood often cannot be aspirated, and the wound keeps bleeding.
  • Stable patient with a wound in the cardiac box: ultrasound of the pericardium; if positive, operative exploration (sternotomy or a subxiphoid pericardial window). A large left hemothorax can decompress pericardial blood into the pleura and make the pericardial view falsely negative, so repeat the study or explore if suspicion stays high.
  • Resuscitative (emergency department) thoracotomy: for a patient with penetrating chest trauma who loses pulses shortly before or after arrival (signs of life recently present). It allows release of tamponade, control of cardiac bleeding, aortic cross-clamping and open cardiac massage. Outcomes are far worse after blunt trauma.

Blunt cardiac injury

StepApproach
Screening12-lead ECG for every patient with significant blunt chest trauma, plus a troponin
Normal ECG and normal troponinBlunt cardiac injury effectively excluded; no cardiac monitoring needed
New ECG abnormality (arrhythmia, conduction block, ST changes) or rising troponinAdmit for continuous ECG monitoring (about 24–48 hours)
Hemodynamic instability or arrhythmia without another explanationEchocardiography (look for wall motion abnormality, effusion, valve or septal injury)

Echocardiography is not a screening test in stable patients. Sternal fracture alone does not predict cardiac injury. Treat arrhythmias in the usual way; heart failure from contusion is managed supportively.

Blunt aortic injury

  • Suspect it after any high-energy deceleration, especially with a widened mediastinum or first-rib, scapular or sternal fractures.
  • Diagnosis: CT angiography of the chest (fast, sensitive, shows other injuries). Transesophageal echocardiography is an alternative in an unstable patient in the operating room. Catheter aortography is mostly historical.
  • Anti-impulse therapy while awaiting repair: lower heart rate first with an IV beta-blocker (esmolol), then blood pressure with a vasodilator if needed; good analgesia. Giving a vasodilator first causes reflex tachycardia, which raises shear on the aortic wall. Do not give anti-impulse therapy to a patient in hemorrhagic shock.
  • Repair: thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) is preferred over open repair for suitable anatomy. Minimal intimal tears can be treated medically with follow-up imaging.
  • Priorities: a contained aortic injury rarely kills in the first hours, whereas active hemorrhage elsewhere does. Control life-threatening bleeding (laparotomy, angioembolisation, pelvic stabilisation) first, then repair the aorta once the patient is stable.

Commotio cordis

Collapse right after a blow to the chest during sport: start CPR and attach an automated external defibrillator immediately. Survival falls quickly with every minute without defibrillation, which is why AEDs and trained staff at youth sports events matter. After survival, evaluate for structural heart disease and channelopathies.

s23b-s-081301-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Surface anatomy that predicts the injury

The right ventricle forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart and lies directly behind the sternum and the left parasternal intercostal spaces, so it is the chamber most often hit by anterior stab wounds and squeezed in blunt trauma. The left ventricle forms the apex and most of the left border; the left atrium is the most posterior chamber, next to the esophagus. A penetrating wound inside the 'cardiac box' (between the midclavicular lines, from the clavicles to the costal margins) should be presumed to involve the heart until proven otherwise.

The pericardium and tamponade

The tough fibrous pericardium is fused with the parietal layer of the serous pericardium; the visceral layer (epicardium) covers the heart. The pericardial space normally holds a small amount of fluid. Because the fibrous sac barely stretches over minutes, as little as 100–200 mL of blood accumulating quickly can cause tamponade, whereas a slowly growing effusion can reach a litre or more before it does.

  • Rising pericardial pressure is transmitted to all chambers, so diastolic pressures in the right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery and left atrium (wedge) equalise.
  • Filling falls, stroke volume falls, and the patient becomes tachycardic and hypotensive with distended neck veins and quiet heart sounds (Beck triad). Hypovolemia from other injuries can hide the neck vein distension.
  • Pulsus paradoxus (an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mm Hg): inspiration increases right-sided filling, and because the total volume inside the sac is fixed, the septum bows toward the left ventricle and left ventricular filling and stroke volume fall.
  • ECG: low voltage and, with large effusions, electrical alternans (the heart swings within the fluid).

Blunt cardiac injury

Sudden compression between sternum and spine (steering wheel, falls, crush) can bruise the myocardium (contusion), injure valves or the septum, or rupture a chamber. Contusion behaves like an infarct without coronary occlusion: myocyte necrosis, troponin release and arrhythmias. The most common findings are sinus tachycardia and premature beats; right bundle branch block also occurs because the right ventricle and septum are anterior. Free wall rupture usually kills at the scene.

Commotio cordis

A low-energy blow to the precordium (a baseball, hockey puck or fist) without structural damage can trigger ventricular fibrillation if it lands during a narrow window on the upstroke of the T wave, when repolarisation is heterogeneous. Stretch-activated ion channels open and produce a premature depolarisation that falls on vulnerable myocardium. Young, compliant chest walls transmit the energy efficiently. Survival depends on immediate CPR and defibrillation.

Blunt aortic injury

Rapid deceleration (high-speed crash, fall from height) lets the mobile ascending aorta and arch keep moving while the descending aorta is held by the ligamentum arteriosum, the intercostal arteries and the pleura. The shear concentrates at the isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian artery where the ligamentum arteriosum attaches. The ligamentum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, derived from the left sixth pharyngeal (aortic) arch. Most people with complete transection die at the scene; survivors usually have a contained tear (pseudoaneurysm) held by the adventitia and surrounding tissue.

Clues on a supine chest radiograph: a widened mediastinum, an indistinct aortic knob, rightward deviation of the trachea or nasogastric tube, depression of the left mainstem bronchus, a left apical pleural cap and a left hemothorax. A normal film does not exclude it.

Iatrogenic ventricular puncture

The thin right ventricular free wall can be perforated by pacing leads, catheters, pericardiocentesis needles or during cardiac procedures. Bleeding into the pericardium causes tamponade, sometimes hours after the procedure. In the subxiphoid approach to pericardiocentesis, the needle passes the skin, the subcutaneous tissue and the diaphragmatic attachments, then the fibrous pericardium with its fused parietal serous layer, aiming toward the left shoulder; advancing too far enters the right ventricle.

Tamponade and tension pneumothorax both cause obstructive shock with distended neck veins. Breath sounds and tracheal position separate them: tension pneumothorax has absent breath sounds on one side and tracheal shift; tamponade has equal breath sounds and muffled heart sounds.

Kussmaul sign (a rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration) is typical of constrictive pericarditis, not acute tamponade; pulsus paradoxus is the classic tamponade sign.

s23b-s-081401-ck-01.bodyHtml:
The cyanotic or shocked newborn

Newborn pulse-oximetry screening (right hand and a foot, after 24 hours of age) detects many critical lesions before discharge; a low saturation or a hand–foot difference prompts echocardiography. Two emergency patterns:

  • Cyanosis that does not rise with 100% oxygen (failed hyperoxia test) suggests a fixed mixing or right-to-left lesion: transposition, pulmonary atresia, critical pulmonary stenosis, tricuspid atresia, tetralogy with severe obstruction.
  • Shock with weak femoral pulses in the first 1–2 weeks as the ductus closes suggests a duct-dependent systemic lesion: critical coarctation, interrupted aortic arch, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, critical aortic stenosis. The differential is sepsis and inborn errors, but a lower-limb saturation or pressure deficit points to the heart.

For either, start prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) as soon as a duct-dependent lesion is suspected; do not wait for echocardiography. Watch for apnea (be ready to intubate), fever, hypotension and flushing. Then obtain echocardiography and transfer to a cardiac center. In transposition with a restrictive atrial septum, balloon atrial septostomy improves mixing; definitive repair is the arterial switch operation in the first weeks.

Tetralogy of Fallot

Diagnosis is by echocardiography. Full surgical repair (VSD patch and relief of outflow obstruction) is usually done in infancy. Hypercyanotic spell management, in order: calm the child and place in the knee-to-chest position (older children squat) with oxygen; then IV fluid bolus, morphine (reduces agitation and hyperpnea), a beta-blocker (relaxes the infundibulum, slows the heart) and an alpha-agonist such as phenylephrine (raises systemic resistance). Avoid inotropes such as dobutamine, which worsen infundibular obstruction. A shunt or urgent repair follows recurrent spells.

Left-to-right shunts in infancy

  • Small VSD (loud murmur, normal growth, normal chamber sizes and pulmonary pressures): reassurance and follow-up; many close spontaneously. No endocarditis prophylaxis is needed.
  • Large VSD with heart failure (tachypnea, sweating with feeds, failure to thrive, hepatomegaly): diuretics and high-calorie feeds as a bridge; surgical closure in infancy, before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease.
  • PDA in a preterm infant: echocardiography confirms the duct and its significance. Many small ducts close on their own and are managed conservatively. A hemodynamically significant duct can be treated with ibuprofen or indomethacin (or acetaminophen); avoid NSAIDs with active bleeding, thrombocytopenia, necrotizing enterocolitis or significant renal impairment. Transcatheter or surgical closure follows failed medical therapy. A PDA beyond infancy in a term child is closed (usually transcatheter) to prevent endarteritis and pulmonary vascular disease, except a tiny silent duct.
  • AV septal defect (Down syndrome): surgical repair at 3–6 months. All infants with Down syndrome need an echocardiogram.

Coarctation of the aorta

Suspect it with upper-limb hypertension, weak or delayed femoral pulses and a lower-limb blood pressure that is lower than the arm pressure. Echocardiography is the initial test (and evaluates the aortic valve, commonly bicuspid); CT or MR angiography defines the anatomy in older children and adults. Treatment is surgical repair (resection with end-to-end anastomosis in infants) or balloon angioplasty with stenting in older children and adults. Lifelong follow-up is needed: hypertension often persists, and recoarctation, aortic aneurysm at the repair site, aortic valve disease and intracranial aneurysm can occur. Screen girls with Turner syndrome with echocardiography or cardiac MRI.

Exam trap: in a cyanotic newborn with suspected duct-dependent disease, the next step is alprostadil, not indomethacin (which closes the duct) and not waiting for the echo.

s23b-s-081401-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Most children with congenital heart disease now reach adulthood, and the population of adults with repaired or unrepaired lesions is larger than the pediatric one. Adults may also present for the first time with lesions that are silent in childhood, especially ASD, bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation.

Atrial septal defect found in adulthood

Presentation: exertional dyspnea, palpitations or atrial fibrillation/flutter, paradoxical embolism, or an incidental fixed split S2, right bundle branch block pattern or right heart enlargement. TTE (with agitated saline) diagnoses most; TEE or cardiac MRI defines anatomy and rims, and right heart catheterization measures the shunt (Qp:Qs) and pulmonary vascular resistance when pulmonary hypertension is suspected.

  • Close an ASD that causes right atrial or ventricular enlargement (a significant shunt, often Qp:Qs ≥ 1.5:1) when pulmonary vascular resistance is not prohibitively high.
  • Transcatheter device closure is preferred for a secundum defect with adequate rims; surgery is needed for primum and sinus venosus defects, coronary sinus defects, and secundum defects unsuitable for a device.
  • Closure is not done when pulmonary vascular disease is severe and the shunt has reversed (Eisenmenger physiology); closing it removes the right ventricle's "pop-off" valve.

Patent foramen ovale

A PFO is present in about a quarter of adults and is usually harmless. After a nonlacunar ischemic stroke with no other cause (cryptogenic) despite a thorough evaluation (vessel imaging, prolonged rhythm monitoring for atrial fibrillation, echocardiography), adults up to about 60 years with a PFO, especially with a large shunt or an atrial septal aneurysm, benefit from percutaneous PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy, which lowers recurrent stroke more than antiplatelet therapy alone. An incidental PFO without a stroke is not closed.

Eisenmenger syndrome

Unrepaired large shunts lead to severe pulmonary vascular disease and shunt reversal. Features: central cyanosis, clubbing, secondary erythrocytosis, hemoptysis, arrhythmias, paradoxical emboli. Management in a specialist center: pulmonary arterial hypertension therapy (for example an endothelin receptor antagonist), treatment of iron deficiency, phlebotomy only for symptomatic hyperviscosity with dehydration excluded, and avoidance of dehydration, high altitude and air in IV lines (use filters). Pregnancy carries a very high maternal mortality and is advised against; estrogen-containing contraception is avoided because of thrombosis risk. Transplant (heart–lung, or lung with repair) is the definitive option.

Repaired lesions

  • Tetralogy of Fallot after repair: chronic pulmonary regurgitation leads to RV dilation; ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death are late risks (QRS duration is a marker). Pulmonary valve replacement is considered for symptoms or progressive RV dilation.
  • Coarctation after repair: monitor blood pressure (including arm–leg gradient), image the aorta periodically for recoarctation or aneurysm, and follow the bicuspid aortic valve.
  • Transposition after an older atrial switch: the RV is the systemic ventricle and often fails; atrial arrhythmias are common. After the arterial switch, watch for neo-aortic root dilation and coronary problems.

Endocarditis prophylaxis in congenital heart disease

Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures that manipulate gingiva is limited to the highest-risk patients: unrepaired cyanotic disease (including palliative shunts and conduits), the first 6 months after complete repair with prosthetic material or a device, repaired disease with a residual defect at or next to prosthetic material, plus anyone with a prosthetic valve, previous endocarditis or a transplanted heart with valvulopathy. An isolated ASD, VSD or PDA does not need prophylaxis.

High yield: secundum ASD with right heart enlargement → transcatheter closure; primum or sinus venosus → surgery; cryptogenic stroke with PFO in an adult under 60 → closure plus antiplatelet; Eisenmenger → no closure, no pregnancy.

s23b-s-081401-s1-01.bodyHtml:
From tube to four chambers

The heart forms from splanchnic mesoderm as a single tube that begins to beat in the fourth week. The tube loops to the right (dextral looping; failure of normal left–right patterning gives dextrocardia, as in primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus). Its segments become the adult structures in a predictable way:

Embryonic segmentAdult derivative
Truncus arteriosusAscending aorta and pulmonary trunk (divided by the aorticopulmonary septum)
Bulbus cordisSmooth outflow parts of both ventricles (conus arteriosus of the RV, aortic vestibule of the LV)
Primitive ventricleTrabeculated parts of both ventricles
Primitive atriumTrabeculated parts of both atria (auricles)
Sinus venosus, left hornCoronary sinus
Sinus venosus, right hornSmooth posterior wall of the right atrium (sinus venarum)
Primitive pulmonary veinSmooth part of the left atrium

Septation

  • Atria. The septum primum grows toward the endocardial cushions, leaving the ostium primum; perforations in its upper part form the ostium secundum. The thicker septum secundum grows to its right, leaving an opening, the foramen ovale. After birth, left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure and presses the septum primum (the flap) against the septum secundum, closing the foramen functionally. Failure of anatomic fusion leaves a patent foramen ovale (about a quarter of adults). Excess resorption of septum primum or a deficient septum secundum gives an ostium secundum ASD; failure of the cushions to meet the septum primum gives an ostium primum ASD.
  • Atrioventricular canal. The superior and inferior endocardial cushions fuse to divide the canal into right and left orifices and contribute to the lower atrial septum, the inlet ventricular septum and the mitral and tricuspid valves. Failure gives an atrioventricular septal (endocardial cushion) defect, characteristic of Down syndrome.
  • Ventricles. The muscular septum grows up from the floor; the final gap is closed by the membranous septum, formed from cushion tissue and the conotruncal ridges. The membranous part is the most common site of VSD.
  • Outflow. Neural crest cells migrate into the truncal and bulbar ridges, which fuse in a spiral to form the aorticopulmonary septum. No septum → persistent truncus arteriosus; a septum that does not spiral → transposition; an unequal division with anterosuperior displacement of the outlet (infundibular) septum → tetralogy of Fallot. Neural crest defects explain why conotruncal lesions travel with 22q11.2 deletion (thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia, hypocalcemia, facial features) and include interrupted aortic arch.

Fetal circulation and the changes at birth

Oxygenated blood returns from the placenta in the umbilical vein (the most saturated fetal blood), partly bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus, and enters the right atrium, where the crista directs it across the foramen ovale to the left heart and the head and arms. Blood from the superior vena cava goes mainly to the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk; because pulmonary vascular resistance is high, most of it crosses the ductus arteriosus (derived from the left sixth arch) into the descending aorta and returns to the placenta in the two umbilical arteries.

At birth, lung expansion lowers pulmonary vascular resistance, and clamping the cord raises systemic resistance. Left atrial pressure exceeds right, closing the foramen ovale. Rising arterial oxygen and the fall in circulating prostaglandin E2 (no longer made by the placenta and now cleared by the lungs) constrict the ductus, which closes within days and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. Remnants: ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum; umbilical vein → ligamentum teres hepatis; umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments; allantois → median umbilical ligament (urachus).

Bridge: prostaglandins keep the ductus open, so alprostadil (PGE1) keeps it open in duct-dependent lesions, and COX inhibitors (indomethacin, ibuprofen) or acetaminophen help close it in preterm infants. NSAIDs taken late in pregnancy can close the fetal ductus prematurely.

Shunt physiology

  • Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, PDA, AV septal defect) are acyanotic at first and raise pulmonary blood flow. Symptoms in infants (tachypnea, sweating with feeds, poor weight gain) appear as pulmonary vascular resistance falls over the first weeks.
  • Chronic high pulmonary flow and pressure remodel the small pulmonary arteries (medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, plexiform lesions). When pulmonary resistance exceeds systemic resistance the shunt reverses (Eisenmenger syndrome): late cyanosis, clubbing, secondary erythrocytosis, a loud P2 and softening of the original murmur. A reversed PDA gives differential cyanosis (blue, clubbed toes, pink fingers) because desaturated blood enters the aorta below the left subclavian artery.
  • Right-to-left shunts cause cyanosis early, often at birth: transposition, tetralogy, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous return, plus hypoplastic left heart and Ebstein anomaly. Cyanosis that does not improve with 100% oxygen points to a fixed intracardiac mixing lesion rather than lung disease.
Exam trap: a paradoxical embolism (venous clot to brain) needs a right-to-left path, usually a PFO with transiently higher right atrial pressure (Valsalva, cough, PE). Do not confuse the PFO (a flap that failed to seal) with a secundum ASD (a true deficiency of tissue).

Acyanotic lesions

LesionFindingsNotes
Ventricular septal defect (most common congenital lesion)Harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; small defects are loudestMany small muscular and membranous defects close spontaneously; large ones cause heart failure in infancy and, untreated, Eisenmenger syndrome
Atrial septal defectWide, fixed split S2; soft systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border (extra flow across the pulmonic valve); a tricuspid flow rumble if largeOften silent until adulthood (exercise intolerance, atrial arrhythmias, right heart enlargement). Secundum is most common; primum is in AV septal defect; sinus venosus defects travel with anomalous pulmonary venous return
Patent ductus arteriosusContinuous "machinery" murmur under the left clavicle; bounding pulses and wide pulse pressureCommon in preterm infants and congenital rubella; closes with COX inhibitors in preterm infants

Cyanotic lesions

  • Tetralogy of Fallot: anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum causes (1) right ventricular outflow obstruction, (2) a large malaligned VSD, (3) an aorta overriding the VSD and (4) right ventricular hypertrophy. The degree of outflow obstruction sets the degree of cyanosis. The murmur is a systolic ejection murmur of the outflow obstruction, not of the VSD. CXR: upturned apex and concave pulmonary segment (boot-shaped heart) with reduced lung markings. Hypercyanotic spells follow crying or exertion; squatting raises systemic vascular resistance, pushing more blood through the pulmonary outflow.
  • Transposition of the great arteries: the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV, giving two parallel circuits. Survival depends on mixing (foramen ovale, ductus, VSD). Severe cyanosis in the first hours, often no murmur, single loud S2; CXR: narrow mediastinum with an egg-shaped heart. Associated with maternal pregestational diabetes.
  • Persistent truncus arteriosus: one vessel overriding a VSD supplies systemic, pulmonary and coronary circulations; linked to 22q11.2 deletion.
  • Tricuspid atresia: needs an ASD and VSD (or PDA) to survive; hypoplastic RV, left axis deviation on ECG.
  • Total anomalous pulmonary venous return: pulmonary veins drain to the systemic venous side; obstructed forms cause severe cyanosis and pulmonary edema in the newborn.
  • Ebstein anomaly: apical displacement of the tricuspid leaflets, "atrialized" RV, tricuspid regurgitation, often an ASD and accessory pathways (WPW). Associated with maternal lithium exposure, although the absolute risk is small.

Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery

When the left coronary artery arises from the pulmonary trunk, it is perfused well enough in fetal life, when pulmonary pressure is high. Over the first weeks after birth, pulmonary pressure falls: the left coronary territory now receives low-pressure, desaturated blood, and once collaterals from the right coronary artery form, flow runs backwards through the left coronary into the low-pressure pulmonary artery (a coronary steal). The infant develops myocardial ischemia at 1–3 months: irritability, pallor and sweating with feeds, heart failure, mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle ischemia, and an anterolateral infarct pattern (deep Q waves in I, aVL, V5–V6) on ECG.

s23b-s-081501-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Cardio-oncology

  • Before an anthracycline or trastuzumab, assess cardiovascular risk and obtain a baseline echocardiogram (left ventricular ejection fraction). Control blood pressure, lipids and diabetes.
  • During trastuzumab, the ejection fraction is typically rechecked about every 3 months. A significant drop (for example, by 10 or more percentage points to below 50%) or symptoms of heart failure → hold trastuzumab, start guideline-directed heart failure therapy, and repeat imaging in about 3–4 weeks; the drug can often be restarted if function recovers.
  • Anthracycline cardiomyopathy is managed like other heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Survivors of childhood cancer treated with anthracyclines or chest radiation need lifelong periodic cardiac surveillance.
  • Chest pain during 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine: stop the infusion, treat vasospasm with nitrates or a calcium channel blocker and evaluate for ischemia.
  • New heart block, arrhythmia or troponin rise on an immune checkpoint inhibitor: suspect myocarditis; hold the drug and give high-dose glucocorticoids promptly.

Cocaine- and amphetamine-associated chest pain

Treat like any possible acute coronary syndrome (ECG, troponin, aspirin), with specific changes:

  • Benzodiazepines first for agitation, tachycardia and hypertension: they reduce central sympathetic outflow.
  • Nitroglycerin and calcium channel blockers for ongoing chest pain or hypertension; phentolamine for refractory hypertension.
  • Avoid β-blockers during acute intoxication (unopposed α-stimulation).
  • ST elevation → primary PCI as for any STEMI.
  • Hyperthermia is a major cause of death: cool aggressively. A wide QRS (Na+ channel blockade) is treated with IV sodium bicarbonate.
  • Offer treatment for substance use disorder before discharge.

Renin–angiotensin system inhibitors

ProblemManagement
ACE inhibitor coughSwitch to an ARB (cough is rare with ARBs). Cough resolves within days to weeks of stopping.
ACE inhibitor angioedemaSecure the airway first; antihistamines, glucocorticoids and epinephrine work poorly because the mechanism is bradykinin, not histamine. Stop the ACE inhibitor permanently and never rechallenge with any ACE inhibitor. Sacubitril-valsartan is contraindicated. Prefer another class (for example a calcium channel blocker or thiazide); an ARB can be used with caution if strongly indicated.
Hyperkalemia or creatinine riseCheck K+ and creatinine 1–2 weeks after starting or raising the dose. A creatinine rise up to about 30% is acceptable; larger rises suggest volume depletion or renal artery stenosis. Stop interacting drugs (NSAIDs, potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim).
PregnancyContraindicated; switch before conception to labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa.

Other common problems

  • Amlodipine edema: lower the dose, or add an ACE inhibitor or ARB; diuretics are largely ineffective. Switching to a nondihydropyridine agent is an alternative if there is no contraindication.
  • Verapamil or diltiazem with a β-blocker: additive bradycardia and AV block, especially in older adults; avoid the combination in conduction disease or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
  • α1 blockers in older men with benign prostatic hyperplasia: start low, at bedtime, and warn about orthostatic dizziness and falls; tell the ophthalmologist before cataract surgery (intraoperative floppy iris).
  • Minoxidil: reserved for resistant hypertension; prescribe with a β-blocker and a loop diuretic and watch for weight gain and pericardial effusion.

Digoxin toxicity

Suspect it in an older patient with renal impairment or a new interacting drug who has nausea, confusion, visual changes or a new arrhythmia. Check the serum digoxin level (at least 6 hours after the last dose), potassium, magnesium and creatinine. Give digoxin-specific antibody fragments for life-threatening arrhythmia, hemodynamic instability, end-organ dysfunction or a high serum potassium in acute ingestion. Correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. Hemodialysis does not remove digoxin (large volume of distribution). For hyperkalemia, Fab treats the cause; insulin–glucose can be used as well.

QT-prolonging drugs in practice

Before adding a QT-prolonging drug in someone at risk (other QT drugs, heart disease, older age, female sex, electrolyte disturbance, bradycardia), check an ECG and electrolytes. A corrected QT above about 500 ms, or an increase of more than about 60 ms, is a reason to stop or avoid the drug and choose an alternative. Common pairings to avoid: methadone with a macrolide or fluoroquinolone; an antipsychotic with ondansetron; citalopram at high doses in older adults.
