s23b-s-081501-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Drugs harm the cardiovascular system in a handful of recurring ways: they damage myocytes, constrict coronary arteries, disturb ion channels (arrhythmias and QT prolongation), retain salt and water, or push blood pressure too far up or down. Recognizing the pattern and the mechanism is the Step 1 task.

Cancer therapy

DrugMain cardiovascular toxicityMechanism and features
Anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunorubicin)Dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failureCumulative dose–dependent myocyte injury from topoisomerase IIβ–mediated DNA damage and iron-dependent free radical generation; can appear years after treatment and is largely irreversible. Risk is higher with older age, chest radiation, pre-existing heart disease and combined trastuzumab. Dexrazoxane, an iron chelator that also interferes with topoisomerase IIβ binding, reduces the risk.
Trastuzumab (anti-HER2 antibody)Fall in ejection fraction, heart failureBlocks HER2 (ERBB2) survival signalling in cardiomyocytes, causing dysfunction (stunning) rather than cell death; not cumulative dose–dependent and usually reversible when the drug is held.
Fluoropyrimidines (5-fluorouracil, capecitabine)Chest pain, ischemia, arrhythmiaCoronary vasospasm, often during or shortly after infusion, with normal coronary anatomy.
Immune checkpoint inhibitorsMyocarditis (can be fulminant), often with myositis or myasthenia-like weaknessT-cell–mediated inflammation; troponin rise, conduction block; treated with high-dose glucocorticoids.
VEGF pathway inhibitors (bevacizumab, multikinase inhibitors)Hypertension, thrombosisReduced nitric oxide production and capillary rarefaction.
High-dose cyclophosphamideAcute hemorrhagic myocarditisEndothelial injury; acute and dose-related.
Chest radiationPremature coronary disease, valve thickening, constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathyFibrosis of all cardiac layers, appearing years to decades later.
Anthracycline vs trastuzumab: anthracycline damage is cumulative, structural (myocyte loss on biopsy) and mostly permanent; trastuzumab dysfunction is not dose-related and recovers after the drug is stopped.

Sympathomimetic drugs of abuse

  • Cocaine blocks presynaptic reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin. Excess norepinephrine at α1 receptors constricts coronary arteries while β1 stimulation raises heart rate and contractility, so oxygen demand rises as supply falls. Cocaine also promotes platelet aggregation and thrombosis, accelerates atherosclerosis, and blocks fast Na+ channels (wide QRS, ventricular arrhythmias). Results: myocardial infarction (even in young people with normal coronaries), aortic dissection, stroke, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy.
  • Amphetamines and methamphetamine release catecholamines from nerve terminals; chronic use causes a dilated cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension.
  • Phencyclidine (PCP) is an NMDA receptor antagonist that also has sympathomimetic effects: hypertension and tachycardia with violent agitation, vertical or rotatory nystagmus and analgesia.
Why β-blockers are avoided in acute cocaine toxicity: blocking β2-mediated vasodilation leaves α1-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which can worsen coronary spasm and hypertension.

Antihypertensives: class-specific adverse effects

ClassAdverse effectMechanism
ACE inhibitorsDry cough; angioedemaACE (kininase II) also degrades bradykinin and substance P; their accumulation causes cough and, more rarely, angioedema (more common in Black patients). Not IgE-mediated.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aldosterone antagonistsHyperkalemia; rise in creatinineLess aldosterone → less K+ secretion by principal cells of the collecting duct; loss of efferent arteriolar constriction lowers GFR, sharply so with bilateral renal artery stenosis. All are teratogenic in the second and third trimesters (renin–angiotensin system inhibitors).
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine)Ankle edema, flushing, headache, reflex tachycardia, gingival hyperplasiaEdema comes from precapillary arteriolar dilation that raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, not from salt retention; diuretics barely help, while adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB (which dilates the venous side) reduces it.
Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem)Bradycardia, AV block, constipation (verapamil), worsening of heart failure with reduced ejection fractionCa2+ channel block in nodal tissue and myocardium; additive with β-blockers.
α1 blockers (prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin)First-dose orthostatic hypotension and syncopeLoss of α1-mediated venous and arteriolar constriction on standing; start low and at bedtime.
MinoxidilHypertrichosis, marked salt and water retention, reflex tachycardia, pericardial effusionOpens ATP-sensitive K+ channels in arteriolar smooth muscle → hyperpolarization → relaxation; given with a β-blocker and a loop diuretic.
HydralazineReflex tachycardia, fluid retention, drug-induced lupus (slow acetylators)Direct arteriolar dilator (raised cGMP).
ClonidineRebound hypertension if stopped abruptlyCentral α2 agonist; sudden loss of sympathetic suppression.

Digoxin toxicity

Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase. Higher intracellular Na+ reduces Ca2+ extrusion by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, increasing contractility; excess intracellular Ca2+ causes delayed afterdepolarizations. Digoxin also increases vagal tone. Toxicity gives nausea, vomiting, anorexia, confusion and visual changes (blurred, yellow-green tinted vision), and almost any arrhythmia combining increased automaticity with impaired conduction: frequent PVCs, bidirectional VT, atrial tachycardia with AV block, and AV block. Acute overdose causes hyperkalemia (pump inhibition throughout the body). Toxicity is precipitated by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, renal failure and drugs that raise digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein or renal clearance (amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine, clarithromycin).

Drug-induced QT prolongation

Most culprit drugs block the hERG channel (IKr): class IA and III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, azole antifungals, methadone, ondansetron, haloperidol and other antipsychotics, citalopram and tricyclic antidepressants. Tricyclics also block fast Na+ channels, widening the QRS, which is treated with sodium bicarbonate.

Other drug–heart interactions worth knowing: nitrates with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) cause profound hypotension; thiazolidinediones and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cause fluid retention and can precipitate heart failure; triptans and ergots cause vasospasm; fluoroquinolones carry a warning for aortic aneurysm and dissection; clozapine can cause myocarditis.
